item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — The Dodgers set their trade deadline sights on one big target and landed him in Tarik Skubal. The two-time Cy Young Award winner will get the call to start Game 1 of the National League Division Series on Saturday at Dodger Stadium against the Atlanta Braves.
Fabian Ardaya at The Athletic was first to report Skubal getting the call in Game 1.
Skubal started two Games 1 with the Detroit Tigers, and in six postseason starts over 2024-25 has a 2.04 ERA with 56 strikeouts against five unintentional walks in 39 2/3 innings, and has lasted at least six innings in all six starts.
When the Dodgers acquired Skubal from the Tigers on August 2, president of baseball operations noted the team's singular focus at this year's trade deadline.
"We were of the mind to be aggressive for one player, and fortunately we were able to line up," Friedman said at the time. "As we've talked about a lot, whenever there's a star-level player available who can really shift championship odds, those are the moments we'll be more aggressive."
Yoshinobu Yamamoto started Game 1 of the 2024 NLDS, and is coming off one of the best postseasons in MLB history, 5-1 with a 1.45 ERA in 37 1/3 innings. That included consecutive complete games in the NLCS and World Series, and he won all three of his appearances in the Fall Classic, including getting the final eight outs of Game 7 one day after starting and pitching six innings to win Game 6.
Blake Snell has five career starts in Game 1, including twice for the Dodgers last year in the wild card round and NLCS. Tyler Glasnow, with four career Game 1 starts, rounds out the rotation.
"To be honest, we can kind of really put all four guys in a hat, and run them out there," manager Dave Roberts said Tuesday.
"Our pitching staff is pretty special, in my opinion," first baseman Freddie Freeman said. "We got four number ones rolling out there, with Yama, Snell, Skubs, and Glasnow."
Skubal has been just about everything the Dodgers could have wanted when they traded for the two-time Cy Young Award winner on August 2. In 10 starts with Los Angeles, the left-hander had a 2.61 ERA and 2.84 xERA with 70 strikeouts and 13 walks in 62 innings.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Dodgers rotation is their greatest strength this October
item.dc:creator: Eric Stephen
item.description: LOS ANGELES — The Dodgers won a championship in 2024 with a decimated starting rotation and dominant bullpen, then flipped the script with a stellar rotation buoying a shaky bullpen to win another title in 2025. "I think this is about as deep of a pitching staff as we've ever had. There's a lot of really good options to work through as a group
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — The Dodgers won a championship in 2024 with a decimated starting rotation and dominant bullpen, then flipped the script with a stellar rotation buoying a shaky bullpen to win another title in 2025. This year the Dodgers might have melded the two heading into October.
"We have a lot of really talented arms," general manager Brandon Gomes said Tuesday. "I think this is about as deep of a pitching staff as we've ever had. There's a lot of really good options to work through as a group."
For now, we'll focus on the rotation, which looks just as strong this year as it did last October, even though Shohei Ohtani hasn't pitched since July 3 and will not pitch this postseason. The Dodgers filled that slot with a two-time Cy Young Award winner, trading for Tarik Skubal on August 2.
Yoshinobu Yamamoto was again the rock of the starting rotation, making every start for the second year in a row. Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow each missed multiple months with a long injured-list stint in season, then returned with enough of a runway to get ready for October. All four put up solid numbers this season.
| Pitcher | Starts | IP | ERA | xERA | BB rate | K rate |
| Skubal | 26 | 158.7 | 2.72 | 2.94 | 4.4% | 30.0% |
| Yamamoto | 28 | 185 | 2.53 | 2.94 | 5.9% | 25.7% |
| Snell | 9 | 62 | 1.90 | 2.17 | 9.2% | 31.8% |
| Glasnow | 13 | 74 | 3.53 | 2.86 | 8.7% | 34.0% |
*Skubal's numbers include Tigers & Dodgers
"To be honest, we can kind of really put all four guys in a hat, and run them out there," manager Dave Roberts said Tuesday.
Last year, Yamamoto, Snell, Ohtani, and Glasnow combined to start all 17 postseason games, and put up a collective 2.55 ERA in 113 innings, with 127 strikeouts and a 28.5-percent strikeout rate. All four of them pitched in Game 7 of the World Series, including Yamamoto getting the final eight outs one day after winning Game 6 as the starter. Yamamoto last October pitched the Dodgers' first two postseason compete games since 1988, and Blake Snell had starts of eight and seven innings as well.
Quality starts are a bit crude, but criticism tends to focus on the minimum requirements — at least six innings, with no more than three earned runs allowed. But across MLB this regular season, teams went 1,094-484 (.693) in games when they got a quality start, with a collective 1.74 ERA from the starters in those games.
This season, the Dodgers led the majors with 83 quality starts, eight more than the next-best team, the Philadelphia Phillies. Those 83 quality starts by the Dodgers this year were their most since 2015, when they got 95 quality starts from a rotation that included the second- and third-place finishers in National League Cy Young Award voting (Zack Greinke, Clayton Kershaw). They were 60-23 (.723) when getting a quality start in 2026.
Dodgers starters last postseason had 10 quality starts, more than any pitching staff since the 2013 Detroit Tigers. Those 10 quality starts in 17 games were one more than the Dodgers had in their previous five postseasons combined, totaling 53 games.
Last postseason, the Dodgers won all 10 of the games in which they received a quality start, with zero or one run allowed by the starter in seven of those games. Two of those quality starts were by Ohtani, but he's replaced in the rotation by Skubal, who last postseason posted three quality starts in his three tries, totaling 36 strikeouts and four runs allowed in his 20 2/3 innings for the Detroit Tigers.
"Watching Tarik Skubal pitch in the playoffs last year was must-see TV. I was in awe, watching the energy, the dominance he exhibited there," Dodgers president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman said in August after trading for Skubal. "I can't wait to see it on our club."

item.title: [New York Post] Dodgers to tab new ace in surprise Game 1 playoff rotation decision
item.dc:creator: Jack Harris
item.description: To begin their quest for a third-straight World Series this postseason, the Dodgers will turn to the one pitcher in their rotation yet to win a championship ring. Tarik Skubal is expected to be named the team’s starter for Game 1 of the National League Division Series against the Atlanta Braves on Saturday, a source with knowledge of the situation told the California Post, giving the reigning two-time Cy Young Award winner and marquee trade deadline acquisition an immediate opportunity to jump-s
item.content:encoded:
To begin their quest for a third-straight World Series this postseason, the Dodgers will turn to the one pitcher in their rotation yet to win a championship ring.
Tarik Skubal is expected to be named the team’s starter for Game 1 of the National League Division Series against the Atlanta Braves on Saturday, a source with knowledge of the situation told the California Post, giving the reigning two-time Cy Young Award winner and marquee trade deadline acquisition an immediate opportunity to jump-start the club’s three-peat bid.
The Dodgers, of course, had no bad options for their playoff opener.
Their rotation includes four pitchers who would be No. 1 options on most other clubs, with Skubal being joined by Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow for this year’s October push.
However, Skubal is set to get the nod, as The Athletic first reported, after increasingly impressive late-season performances with the Dodgers following his blockbuster arrival from the Detroit Tigers in August.
The 29-year-old left-hander posted a 5-2 record and 2.61 ERA in 10 post-deadline starts with the club, improving upon the 7-5 mark and 2.79 ERA he had with the Tigers during a first half that was sidetracked by an elbow procedure that sidelined him for all of May.
Skubal’s best outings came in the final weeks of the regular season, when he spun a pair of scoreless seven-inning starts in two of his final three appearances of the campaign.
Prior to Friday’s news, there was a thought that Yamamoto would be the Dodgers’ Game 1 starter, given his World Series MVP heroics last fall.
But Yamamoto threw extensively in a simulated game on Wednesday, during the club’s bye week workouts. That kept him on his customary once-per-week pitching schedule (his regular-season finale came on the Wednesday before that) and might line him up to pitch in Game 3 in Atlanta next Tuesday instead. Of note: Yamamoto has notably better splits on the road (1.77 ERA) than at home (3.13 ERA) this year.
Snell, who has followed Skubal in the Dodgers’ rotation lately, seems like the logical candidate to start Game 2 on Sunday. Glasnow, who pitched in another simulated game Thursday, figures to go in Game 4, and could be an option out of the bullpen this weekend.
While Skubal –– who will be the sport’s top free agent this winter –– has yet to win a World Series, he does have a sterling postseason track record.
In six playoff outings over the last two years with the Tigers, he pitched to a 2.04 ERA while striking out 56 batters in 39 ⅔ innings. Those numbers would be even better if not for his one October clunker, when he gave up five runs in a winner-take-all loss in Game 5 of the 2024 American League Division Series.
That failure has become a motivator for Skubal in the two years since. It has left him with a feeling of unfinished business as he begins another playoff campaign amid new surroundings now.
“Once the months change and the playoffs start, nothing matters,” he said last week. “It’s just about winning that game, and that’s how I treat every single start. Because I’m just trying to put our team in a position to win a baseball game. That won’t change from today, and whenever my next start is.”

item.title: [CBS Sports] Should the Phillies trade Bryce Harper or Kyle Schwarber? Why blockbuster deal doesn't make sense
item.dc:creator: Matt Snyder
item.description: The Phillies were bounced from the playoffs with a Game 3 Wild Card Series loss to the Braves on Thursday night. Given that the Phillies made the World Series in 2022 and have regressed in playoff performance since (NLCS in 2023, NLDS in 2024, NLDS in 2025 and WCS in 2026) along with a relatively old roster, there has been a stream of "end of an era" discussion on Friday. It's not unreasonable. There are certainly . There are bound to be overreactions. I overreact a decent amount of the time, so
item.content:encoded:
The Phillies were bounced from the playoffs with a Game 3 Wild Card Series loss to the Braves on Thursday night. Given that the Phillies made the World Series in 2022 and have regressed in playoff performance since (NLCS in 2023, NLDS in 2024, NLDS in 2025 and WCS in 2026) along with a relatively old roster, there has been a stream of "end of an era" discussion on Friday.
It's not unreasonable. There are certainly . There are bound to be overreactions. I overreact a decent amount of the time, so I get it. It happens. We're often prisoners of the moment and emotion is a real thing.
I do want to push back on a specific idea, though, as floated by Ken Rosenthal of The Athletic:
Trading Bryce Harper or Kyle Schwarber? Don't love the idea, but everything needs to be under consideration. Everything.
Now, be sure that this isn't to attack the writer there, as I have the utmost respect for him and he even said he doesn't love the idea. I can see a lot of people running with this, though, and I'll offer up my opinion that this just isn't a feasible idea for the Phillies.
First off, Harper has a no-trade clause and it's been pretty clear over the last several years that he's now Philly through-and-through and doesn't want to go anywhere. Schwarber also has a no-trade clause with his 10-and-5 rights and now has a family with two young children.
Let's say either or both would accept a trade. Would it help the Phillies other than salary relief?
Schwarber is a 34-year-old designated hitter heading into 2027 with four years and $132 million left on his deal. How many teams would give the Phillies anything of value while also taking on a large portion of the salary? The answer is not that many and it might be zero.
Harper needs to permanently go back to first base and he'll also be 34 years old next season. He has five years and roughly $125 million left on his deal. Again, how many teams would give good value back to the Phillies and salary relief? The number is higher than with Schwarber, but not by much.
This isn't to say neither player is good. Both are very productive offensively. In fact, they were the Phillies' only two good hitters this season. Harper had a 131 OPS+ and Schwarber was at 128 with 100 being the average player at getting on base and hitting for power. No other qualified players on the Phillies were in the vicinity of Harper or Schwarber. Only Bryson Stott at 98 even approached league average. Brandon Marsh finished at 90, Alec Bohm 87 and Trea Turner 81. Yuck.
Schwarber and Harper are much more valuable to the Phillies than they would be to any other team, given the circumstances. And, unless the Phillies are going full-on rebuild, they might as well play out the contracts and try to win with them.
If you look at how things are set up for next season with the pitching staff, a rebuild doesn't make sense.
- Jesús Luzardo made a turn toward ace this season. He's under team control through at least 2031.
- Cristopher Sánchez will likely finish in the top three of Cy Young voting. He's under team control through at least 2032.
- Zack Wheeler showed flashes of being really good while returning from an incredibly tough surgical procedure. He's signed for one more season. He could well return to ace form.
- Aaron Nola doesn't have a tradeable deal, but hey, he had a 10-start stretch with a 2.10 ERA late in the season.
- There were still inconsistencies, but Andrew Painter, at age 23, made big strides during the season and perhaps turned a corner with in Game 2 vs. the Braves. Next year could well be a breakout.
That's a five-man rotation and maybe one of the very best in the majors.
Jhoan Duran is a top-three closer, too.
The starting point here is a great rotation and closer combination, along with Harper and Schwarber being excellent hitters. That's a better nucleus than most teams have. Ownership is committed to doing what it takes to land a winner for the city of Philadelphia and Dave Dombrowski is a front office executive who has proven he's good at making good teams into champions.
Keep taking as many shots at the postseason as possible in hopes that one of these years, the hot streak lines up properly for a championship. We've seen a well-timed hot streak pay off in recent years for teams like the Nationals, Braves and Rangers -- and maybe it'll be the Padres this year? -- so we know it can happen. Hell, the 2022 Phillies were right there.
The team defense needs to improve and there should be some tinkering with the position players, but the foundation here is far too strong to bail on Schwarber and/or Harper, especially when it wouldn't improve the big-league roster in the near-term.

item.title: [Diario AS] Dodgers NLDS roster: Who will make the 26-man playoff roster against the Braves?
item.dc:creator: Rodrigo Serrano; Jennifer Bubel
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers have won the National League West for the fifth consecutive season and for the 13th time in the last 14 years. The only team to interrupt their run was the San Francisco Giants in 2021. Since then, no one has been able to take the division away from Los Angeles. Now the defending back-to-back World Series champions are preparing for the National League Division Series, where they will face the Atlanta Braves beginning Saturday at Dodger Stadium. Atlanta advanced by defeat
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers have won the National League West for the fifth consecutive season and for the 13th time in the last 14 years. The only team to interrupt their run was the San Francisco Giants in 2021. Since then, no one has been able to take the division away from Los Angeles.
Now the defending back-to-back World Series champions are preparing for the National League Division Series, where they will face the Atlanta Braves beginning Saturday at Dodger Stadium. Atlanta advanced by defeating the Philadelphia Phillies in the Wild Card Series, setting up the Dodgers’ first postseason matchup with the Braves since the 2021 NL Championship Series.
Your 2026 Los Angeles Dodgers. pic.twitter.com/XYs9LzjRIb
— Los Angeles Dodgers (@Dodgers) September 24, 2026
The Dodgers’ five-day bye gave Dave Roberts and his staff time to prepare their roster, and while most of the pieces are already in place, there are still some important decisions to make before the 26-man NLDS roster is finalized. MLB reports that the final bench spot remains particularly unsettled, while the bullpen could also have an opening depending on the health of Edgardo Henriquez.
Who will make the Dodgers’ pitching staff?
The Dodgers’ biggest strength heading into October is their starting rotation. Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell, and Tyler Glasnow form a formidable group, although Roberts had not formally announced the order entering Friday.
Yamamoto is the leading candidate to start Game 1 against Atlanta. His normal rest schedule is one of the reasons the Japanese right-hander makes the most sense for the opener, as starting Saturday would also give him the chance to be available for a potential Game 5 on his usual rest.
#ITFDB presented by Toyo Tires. pic.twitter.com/TcKpliJrnR
— Los Angeles Dodgers (@Dodgers) September 24, 2026
The Dodgers also have several pitchers who could be used in relief despite spending much of the regular season as starters. Roki Sasaki, Justin Wrobleski and Emmet Sheehan are among the options who could give Roberts additional flexibility out of the bullpen.
Edgardo Henriquez is another name to watch. The right-hander emerged as an important leverage option during the regular season before lower back discomfort ended his year prematurely. The Dodgers planned to have him face hitters during the bye, with an activation for the NLDS possible if he comes through the workout without any problems.
What will the Dodgers’ offense look like?
Shohei Ohtani will once again be the centerpiece of the Dodgers’ offense, but the situation is different from what it appeared to be when the original story was written.
Ohtani returned from the injured list in late September and played in each of the Dodgers’ final five regular-season games. He went 5-for-21 with eight strikeouts and one walk during that stretch, but Roberts said the team had no health concerns with its superstar heading into the postseason.
It’s Shotime! On this day in 2024, Shohei Ohtani started the 50/50 club.
This MomenTito’s in Dodger history presented by Tito's Handmade Vodka. pic.twitter.com/cxOEcJyPNK
— Los Angeles Dodgers (@Dodgers) September 19, 2026
Ohtani is expected to remain the designated hitter, with Mookie Betts at shortstop, Freddie Freeman at first base and Max Muncy at third. The Dodgers’ outfield is also largely established, with Kyle Tucker, Teoscar Hernández and Andy Pages expected to occupy the three spots.
The lineup could continue to feature some adjustments depending on the opposing starter. Against right-handed pitching, Ohtani has been used at the top of the order, while Betts has taken the leadoff spot against left-handers. That platoon is expected to continue into October.
Who's your Player of the Game? Comment your answer below! pic.twitter.com/tt6sVtGvWT
— Los Angeles Dodgers (@Dodgers) September 26, 2026
Who gets the final roster spot?
The Dodgers have several candidates competing for what could be their final bench spot: Josue De Paula, Dalton Rushing, Alex Call, and Hyeseong Kim. MLB’s postseason preview identified the decision as one of the biggest remaining questions for the club.
De Paula is intriguing after his impressive first taste of the Majors. The Dodgers’ top prospect hit .323 with seven RBIs and seven runs scored in 11 games before being optioned to Triple-A when Ohtani returned from the injured list. His performance was strong enough to keep him in the postseason conversation.
But Kim offers something different. His defensive versatility, speed, and ability to contribute off the bench could make him valuable in a playoff series, particularly if Roberts wants another defensive option late in games.
MLB.com Dodgers beat reporter Sonja Chen noted that both De Paula and Kim could have a chance to make the NLDS roster if Los Angeles carries 14 position players and 12 pitchers. The final decision could ultimately come down to whether the Dodgers prefer another impact bat or additional speed and defense.
Rushing and Call remain possibilities as well, meaning the Dodgers have not simply decided between De Paula and Kim.
The other variable is the pitching staff. If Los Angeles carries only 12 pitchers rather than the maximum 13, it would open another position-player spot and potentially allow Roberts to keep more of those candidates.
Dodgers are chasing history
There is plenty more than a division title at stake for Los Angeles. The Dodgers are attempting to become the first team since the New York Yankees from 1998-2000 to win three consecutive World Series titles. They have already won three of the past six championships and enter October as the defending champions for the second straight year.
Their first obstacle is now set: the Atlanta Braves. The two teams will meet Saturday in Game 1 of the NLDS at Dodger Stadium, with Yamamoto the likely starter for Los Angeles. Before the first pitch, however, Roberts and the Dodgers still have a handful of decisions to make about exactly which players will be part of their attempt at a historic three-peat.

item.title: [FanSided] MLB Power Rankings: Every remaining playoff team after Wild Card Round
item.dc:creator: Christopher Kline
item.description: With the exception of Braves-Phillies (of course), this year's Wild Card round was pretty lopsided. The competition should heat up in the Divisional Series, however. Not only are the best teams in each league being reintroduced, but we have division rivals and compelling stylistic contrasts. item.content:encoded:
With the exception of Braves-Phillies (of course), this year's Wild Card round was pretty lopsided. The competition should heat up in the Divisional Series, however. Not only are the best teams in each league being reintroduced, but we have division rivals and compelling stylistic contrasts.
The Brewers and Padres could not be more different in how their teams were built. The Rays and Yankees don't like each other. The Guardians and White Sox also don't like each other. As for Braves-Dodgers? Well, there's plenty of recent history there. But which teams have the look of title contenders as we move deeper into October? Let's rank all eight remaining teams in terms of championship equity.
8. Chicago White Sox
The White Sox made it hard on themselves down the stretch, but Chicago is riding high after a first-round sweep of the Astros, with blessings from the Pope. Coming into the postseason, the White Sox were broadly dinged for their youth and inexperience. As fate would have it, though, the South Siders were significantly more poised than a seasoned Astros team.
Chicago's lineup performed top to bottom. They worked deep into counts and made smart, situational swings. The rotation is still a mess, and the bullpen is not much better, but there's a lovable underdog quality to this White Sox team that is hard to ignore. By default, the White Sox rank last here, but an ALDS matchup with the Guardians is perfectly winnable. Do not discount the possibility of a South Siders pennant run.
7. Cleveland Guardians
Cleveland has been there and done that. This team is always the AL Central champ, it feels like, even when the odds are stacked against them. The Guardians hit much better down the stretch after a brutal start to the campaign, while their pitching is a potential superpower. Parker Messick and Gavin Williams can match just about any aces blow-for-blow, and this bullpen always tends to perform.
The question now becomes: Can Stephen Vogt's squad translate their signature Guards Ball style to October? The answer for years now has been "no." Cleveland lacks thump in the heart of the order, but tends to execute the small things — bunts, base-running, two-strike hitting — better than anyone. Chicago's pitching staff is vulnerable and the Guardians have the edge in experience, but so did Houston. And the Astros' bats were much better. The outcome of this series will not shock me in either direction, to be frank.
6. Atlanta Braves
The Braves lineup struggled down the stretch but appeared to wake up against the Phillies, especially in the clincher. Atlanta has no shortage of offensive talent and a deep bullpen, with plenty of postseason experience to draw on. So why ranked so low?
Well, the rotation is a mess. Chris Sale is an elite 1A, but Tyler Mahle is questionable against better offensive teams (see: Dodgers) and their third starter is Grant Holmes behind an opener. Atlanta has seven starters on the IL and could struggle to build a bridge to the stellar back end of their bullpen in non-Sale starts. That said, if the Braves' bats heat up, perhaps it does not matter. There is a clear break in quality between Cleveland at No. 7 and the rest of the field. The Braves are very, very capable of mounting a deep run. Atlanta notably went 5-1 against the Dodgers this season.
5. Tampa Bay Rays
The Rays just kept winning all season long. There was no more consistent force in the American League. We can quibble with the back half of their lineup and question the depth of their rotation, but the Rays are an extremely disciplined club with star power (Junior Caminero) and fundamental skills (Chandler Simpson, Jonny DeLuca) in equal measure.
Tampa is going to defend at a high level and run the bases with intent. Their pitching staff does not look so fearsome on paper, but Drew Rasmussen is a bonafide ace and Freddy Peralta looked more like himself in September. Whether this team can match the raw explosiveness of the Yankees' lineup is the swing factor. On the flip side, New York has a propensity for unforced errors that Tampa can ruthlessly capitalize on.
4. New York Yankees
The Yankees are still waiting on Aaron Judge. New York stuffed its Wild Card roster with platoon bats and situational hitters, but Aaron Boone probably needs more pitchers for a five-game Divisional Series. The lineup exploded against the Red Sox, but Tampa will almost certainly manage its pitching staff better than Chad Tracy and Boston did.
New York is the best team in the American League on paper, even with all their injuries, but the bullpen is perilously thin and it's hard to trust this lineup completely. Ben Rice has caught fire at an optimal moment, so there's that. And the Yankees boast, by far, the most star power of any team west of Los Angeles. Whether it can all come together against a healthy, well-rested Rays team remains to be seen.
3. Milwaukee Brewers
The Brewers, almost without fail, dominate the regular season despite ownership's pervasive cheapness. This team knows how to develop talent in-house and locate value on the margins. There is no better-run small-market clubhouse in MLB. And yet, Milwaukee has consistently fallen flat in the playoffs. Whether or not this year is any different comes down to a couple factors.
First, Jacob Misiorowski helps. Milwaukee has the best pitcher in baseball and he may damn near guarantee a Game 1 win in the NLDS. The Brewers' bullpen is rock solid, too, while the depth of their rotation is respectable. Milwaukee's pitching can win ballgames. More importantly, there's less elite competition than usual; even the Dodgers are scuttling at the plate, while the entire American League is poked full of holes. The path has never been clearer for the Brewers, who compensate for limited slug with impressive plate discipline and savvy situational hitting. If Milwaukee can maintain its extraordinarily high baseline, there's reason to believe this could be the year it all clicks.
2. San Diego Padres
There are few stars I trust more in a high-leverage spot than Fernando Tatis Jr. The man just makes good things happen, whether he's using his power or his speed. San Diego's entire lineup, really, has come on strong in the final month. After sputtering for much of the regular season, the likes of Jackson Merrill and Manny Machado have apparently remembered how talented they are. Gavin Sheets and Ty France are improbably major contributors. On the pitching front, Michael King and Nick Pivetta tore through a loaded Cubs lineup. The Padres' bullpen is the best in baseball, so no team can more easily build a bridge between their frontline starters and the ninth inning.
San Diego's rotation depth is suspect; once Walker Buehler and Robbie Ray are asked to carry several innings, it could get dicey. But in terms of momentum and top shelf star power, the Padres clear the majority of the competition around them. It can't hurt that San Diego plays the Dodgers as well as any team, either. That matchup could ultimately define the 2026 season, assuming the Padres can out-slug the No. 1 seed Brewers.
1. Los Angeles Dodgers
This shouldn't come as a shock. The Dodgers aren't as untouchable as their reputation suggests, but there's still only one team with Tarik Skubal, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow lined up on the mound. Meanwhile, Shohei Ohtani has proven his capacity for clutch swings time after time since arriving in Hollywood two years ago. Los Angeles has the best pitchers and the best player in MLB, with a star-studded lineup to boot. Mookie Betts, Kyle Tucker and Freddie Freeman weren't at the peak of their powers this season, but that's still a group worth trusting when every at-bat is magnified.
Los Angeles has depth, too. Josue De Paula is one of the most exciting young bats in baseball and the Dodgers barely have room for him on the roster. Alex Call and Dalton Rushing are useful as situational hitters. The primary concern is L.A.'s bullpen, but Rōki Sasaki, Kris Bubic and Justin Wrobleski — their excess rotation arms — should help the Dodgers cover innings when needed. The Dodgers are banged-up and very much vulnerable, but this is still the team to beat, full stop.

item.title: [Bozeman Daily Chronicle] Bryce Harper after Phillies' early playoff exit: 'You're here to win games, and we didn't'
item.dc:creator: BILL TROCCHI
item.description: ATLANTA (AP) — Bryce Harper doesn't play the shoulda, woulda, coulda game. The bottom line for the Philadelphia Phillies is they came up short in the postseason again. “You’re here to do business. You’re here to win games, and we didn’t do that,” Harper said in a subdued Phillies clubhouse Thursday night following their 6-2 loss to the Atlanta Braves in the deciding Game 3 of their National League Wild Card Series. item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA (AP) — Bryce Harper doesn't play the shoulda, woulda, coulda game.
The bottom line for the Philadelphia Phillies is they came up short in the postseason again.
“You’re here to do business. You’re here to win games, and we didn’t do that,” Harper said in a subdued Phillies clubhouse Thursday night following their 6-2 loss to the Atlanta Braves in the deciding Game 3 of their National League Wild Card Series.
There would be no excuses coming from the All-Star slugger about a September swoon that prevented the Phillies from lining up their pitching against Atlanta because it took until Game 162 to clinch a playoff spot.
Philadelphia forced Game 3 against the Braves with three dramatic solo home runs late in Game 2. But in the end, the Phillies fell into an early hole Thursday and were eliminated from the postseason for the fifth consecutive year as they chase their first World Series title since 2008.
“You’d love to be able to set your pitching up and them be rested and all that kind of stuff,” interim manager Don Mattingly said. “But that’s not the way it went. We had to fight to get ourselves in, and to do what we had to do to get in, we had to do what we had to do basically every game in the series.”
The Phillies' core of Harper, Kyle Schwarber, J.T. Realmuto, Zack Wheeler and Aaron Nola have made five straight playoff appearances and averaged 91 wins per year during that stretch. They have yet to win a championship and have been eliminated further and further from that goal each season since reaching the 2022 World Series.
The following season, Philadelphia exited in the National League Championship Series, and the next two years saw losses in the Division Series. A wild-card exit this season marks another step in the wrong direction.
“Obviously, we'd love to win a World Series with these guys. We’ve been together quite a while, and we've got a good clubhouse, and you know, good characters on this team,” Nola said. “We know what type of guys are in here. We know what type of players we have, and what we’re capable of. (We need to) kind of play good at the right time.”
The five-year run included two playoff series wins over the Braves. Philadelphia eliminated Atlanta in 2022 and 2023 despite the Braves winning the NL East in both seasons. That scenario was set up again this year, with the Braves earning home-field advantage in this series by virtue of another NL East title.
This time, however, Atlanta managed to get the big hits and the clutch pitching when it mattered most. Ray Kerr, in just his 10th appearance this year and first career postseason appearance, played the role of opener to perfection. He went 3 1/3 innings, giving up no runs, one walk and one hit to set up bulk reliever Grant Holmes.
Michael Harris II belted a three-run homer off Nola in the first, and the Phillies were looking up the rest of the night.
The Phillies were looking up at the rest of their division in April, but eventually righted the ship. Mattingly took over when Rob Thomson was fired on April 28 after a 9-18 start. The Phillies won eight of their next nine and reached .500 on May 16. A red-hot August put them in playoff position, but a postseason berth was not secured until the final game of the regular season.
Mattingly deflected questions about his future after the game.
“It’s not the time to talk about it. I’m comfortable with whatever they want to do,” he said. “Again, I want the best for the Phillies. I loved being in Philly this year. I actually like playing in that environment. I like the environment. It’s a rough environment, but it’s good. Again, I think you let the organization evaluate, talk about what they think moving forward, what they should do, and that dictates a lot of different things.”
As the clubhouse emptied out for the final time this season, Wheeler reflected on the journey the Phillies went on and the disappointing ending it delivered.
“It is tough. We spent a lot of time together. We see everybody’s ups and downs,” he said. “We see the good times and bad times people have throughout the season. We’re all brothers here, and we love to compete. So something like this happens, it’s tough.”

item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA – While the Phillies tried to extend their season Thursday night against the Atlanta Braves at Truist Park, their Delta 757 charter sat 23 miles away at Hartsfield-Jackson International airport.
A win would send the Phillies west, to Los Angeles and a second straight National League Division Series matchup with the Dodgers.
A loss would send them home, to Philadelphia and another long, cold winter.
It didn’t take long to figure out which way the Phillies would be heading. Aaron Nola was tagged for three runs in the first inning. The Phillies never recovered. Their season came to an end in a 6-2 loss to the Braves in Game 3 of the NL Wild Card Series.
For just the second time in franchise history, the Phillies qualified for the postseason for a fifth straight year, matching a team-high streak first reached from 2007 to 2011. The Phils won the World Series in 2008, but have not since. They made a surprising run to the World Series in 2022 but were beaten by the Houston Astros in six games. They were a win away from returning to the World Series in 2023 only to collapse and lose Games 6 and 7 of the NL Championship Series at home to Arizona. Since then, they have gone the wrong way, losing in the Division Series (their first round of play) in 2024 and 2025 and now in the Wild Card Series.
“It’s always frustrating,” Kyle Schwarber said in the quiet of the losing clubhouse. “From every postseason I’ve been in, it always hurts when you’re not the last team standing.
“It’s just as frustrating this year as it was last year and the year before that.”
Philadelphia Phillies
Complete coverage of the Fightin' Phils and their MLB rivals from NBC Sports Philadelphia.
As the October defeats have mounted, the team’s core group of high-priced veteran players has gotten older.
Schwarber, always the optimist, insisted that the team’s championship window is still wide open. So did J.T. Realmuto, saying, “There’s definitely the talent in this room to win. If you watched us play all year, no matter who we played, we weren’t outmatched. It’s about execution. It’s not about the age and the years. We know we still have the talent to win.”
Over on the other side of the clubhouse, Bryce Harper didn’t sound so sure.
He was asked what gives him faith that the team can still get to where it wants to go.
“Yeah, I don’t know,” he said. “It’s going to be a long offseason, obviously. I have trust in the organization and the people that are in charge. We’ll see where we go.”
Heading into the offseason, the Phils have many questions, first and foremost: Will Don Mattingly return as manager in 2027? He took over, with an interim tag, for Rob Thomson after the team got off to a 9-19 start in April.
The Phillies played .590 ball (79-55) under Mattingly, but president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski tried to hire Alex Cora when he let Thomson go, and he seems likely to try again in the coming weeks. Stay tuned.
Mattingly would not touch the topic after the game. Schwarber, Realmuto, Nola and Trea Turner all said they’d like to see Mattingly return. Harper declined to talk about the topic.
If Cora comes on board, he will be taking over a team of highs and lows, one with an inconsistent offense that is seemingly up one month (see August) and down the next (see September). He will be taking over a team that lacks pitching depth, both in the starting rotation and the bullpen. Both weaknesses reared their head in recent weeks as the Phils had to scramble to make the playoffs, using ace Zack Wheeler on the final day of the regular season, a circumstance that prevented him from starting Game 1 of the postseason.
Wheeler mentioned the team’s overall inconsistency when asked if he believed the Phils still had the talent to make a deeper postseason run next year.
“Consistency in every group, I think that’s what will get us there,” he said. “We were kind of inconsistent throughout the year. Maybe we were hitting, but we weren’t pitching well. Maybe we were pitching well and we weren’t hitting well. We just have to put it all together throughout the majority of the season.
“We’re hungry, that’s for sure. We just didn’t get the job done.”
The Phils had chances to win the series.
Jesus Luzardo pitched well in Game 1 and they held a 3-2 lead in the seventh. With few trusted arms in his leaky bullpen, Mattingly went to his All-Star closer, Jhoan Duran, in the bottom of the seventh. Duran got through that inning but gave up the lead on a three-run homer in the eighth and the Phillies lost, 5-3.
They bounced back to win a wild Game 2 Wednesday in 10 innings on the strength of three late home runs and the clutch pitching of Cristopher Sanchez, Alex McFarlane and Andrew Painter. They seemed to have momentum heading into Game 3.
But the momentum disappeared quickly as Nola had big trouble throwing strikes.
Just three of the right-hander's first 13 pitches to open the game were strikes. He fell behind Ronald Acuna Jr., and Matt Olson, the Braves’ Nos. 2 and 3 hitters, with 3-0 counts and eventually walked both. He then fell behind Michael Harris II, 2-0. Harris hit the next pitch, a sinker down and out of the zone, over the right-field wall for a three-run homer.
“I think he was just a little too careful,” Realmuto said of Nola. “I don’t think he was way off because he was just missing. They just did a good job of not chasing and making him come in the zone. When a lineup is good like that and they get on a roll, it’s tough to get them out when they’re not chasing.”
Nola did not make it through the second inning. Tim Mayza got the final out of the frame before handing off to Wheeler in the top of the third. The Phillies’ brain trust opted not to start Wheeler on three days’ rest. He'd never done that before. Also, Wheeler admitted that at this point of the season, he wasn’t feeling 100 percent. It was decided that Nola’s best chance of succeeding would be to stay in a starter’s role.
“We’re going to need Nola in this game,” Mattingly said before the game. “Starting him gives us the best version of him.”
The Phillies weren’t sure Wheeler would even be able to pitch until he tested himself by playing catch before the game. He ended up pitching four innings but was not particularly sharp. He gave up three hits and walked three. One of those walks turned into a run when Ozzie Albies stroked a two-run homer in the fourth to give the Braves a 5-0 lead.
“We felt Nola was on solid rest,” Mattingly said after the game. “If he could get us into the game at all, we’d have Zack after that. Obviously, it didn’t go well.”
Atlanta used lefty Ray Kerr as an opener. He pitched 3 1/3 innings and did not allow a run. The only hit Kerr gave up was a single to Schwarber in the first inning. Kerr then struck out Harper.
Grant Holmes, Robert Suarez, Didier Fuentes, Dylan Dodd and Chris Sale finished off the Phillies. Sale, the Braves’ ace lefty who started Game 1, entered with two outs in the eighth and struck out Harper.
Before the 2019 season, Harper signed a 13-year, $330-million contract with the Phillies. He came looking for a parade down Broad Street. Eight years later, he boarded a flight back to Philadelphia, still looking.

item.content:encoded:
MLB playoff predictions 2026: Expert picks for every ALDS, NLDS series originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
October has officially arrived, just in time for the MLB postseason to ramp up.
With all four Wild Card series now over — three of which ended in two-game sweeps — just eight teams remain alive in the pursuit of a World Series title, with the Guardians, Rays, Dodgers and Brewers entering the picture after watching the first round from home.
Some of baseball's biggest stars, from Shohei Ohtani and Jacob Misiorowski to Junior Caminero and Cam Schlittler, will be on full display for the division series. On both sides of the bracket, the question will be whether the teams carrying their Wild Card momentum can now take down a well-rested heavyweight.
With a chance to reset between rounds, the best-of-five ALDS and NLDS matchups begin Saturday. Who will advance to the championship series?
With Wild Card matchups in the rearview mirror, The Sporting News predicts the 2026 MLB division series matchups.
MORE: Complete MLB playoff schedule for 2026 postseason
No. 6 Chicago White Sox vs. No. 2 Cleveland Guardians
You can certainly debate whether the Guardians (85 regular-season wins) or White Sox (84 regular-season wins) really belong on the postseason stage this season, with neither AL Central squad owning a ton of big-name star power. Regardless, the fact is that Cleveland and Chicago both find themselves with an opportunity to make a serious postseason run in a weaker AL bracket — and the White Sox have already taken advantage.
Chicago enters the ALDS the momentum of its first postseason series win since the 2005 World Series, proving in the Wild Card round that it has the power and pitching depth to challenge opponents. Cleveland, though, has better top-end starting pitching in Parker Messick, Gavin Williams and Tanner Bibee.
These two teams are well familiar with each other; the White Sox won the season series, 7-6. Cleveland's offense isn't very threatening, ranking last among all postseason teams in team OPS (.696) — this matchup will likely come down to how early the White Sox's bats can get to Guardians starters.
Saturday will mark the first time in MLB history that the Chicago White Sox and Cleveland have met in the postseason.
The White Sox began playing baseball in 1894 as the Sioux City Cornhuskers.
The Guardians began playing baseball in 1896 as the Columbus Buckeyes/Senators.
The fact that this is a divisional matchup means it will likely be close, but Chicago's momentum is hard to ignore, and there was only a one-win discrepancy between the sides in the regular season. The White Sox are finally building something serious, seemingly with a new hero every night. The power in Will Venable's lineup is dangerous enough to reach the ALCS.
Prediction: White Sox in 4
No. 4 New York Yankees vs. No. 1 Tampa Bay Rays
It's been clear since the start of the postseason that whichever AL East team emerged from the lower half of the bracket would be favored to reach the World Series. This is the heavyweight matchup of the two ALDS series, featuring elite starting pitching on both sides and some of MLB's premiere sluggers.
Of course, the massive question lingering over this matchup is how much, if at all, Aaron Judge will play for the Yankees. Even as the lower seed, if he's near 100 percent, it's hard not to view New York as the favorite to reach the ALCS; a healthy Judge, alongside Cody Bellinger, Luis Garcia Jr. and Ben Rice, takes Aaron Boone's lineup to a new level, capable of matching the all-around offensive excellence of Tampa Bay's quartet: Caminero, Yandy Siaz, Jonathan Aranda and Chandler Simpson.
The Rays won this season series 7-6, but it may be the most evenly matched division series. Both sides can roll out a trio talented starters — New York with Cam Schlittler, Max Fried and Gerrit Cole, and Tampa Bay with Drew Rasmussen, Nick Martinez and Shane McClanahan — to pair with deep offenses.
Yankees can line up their pitching as follows against the Rays:
Game 1: Gerrit Cole
Game 2: Cam Schlittler
Game 3: Max Fried
Game 4: Gerrit Cole
Game 5: Cam Schlittler
For two reasons, the Yankees are the pick here. For one, between Schlittler and arguably the best bullpen in baseball, New York is loaded with leverage arms. And the Yankees are also riding high off a dominant Wild Card series, biding time for Judge and Giancarlo Stanton to heal. Assuming those two sluggers can at least be used in some key at-bats, the Yankees' lineup is capable of changing games in an instant.
Prediction: Yankees in 5
No. 3 Atlanta Braves vs. No. 2 Los Angeles Dodgers
The Dodgers' path to becoming the first National League team to win three-straight World Series will begin with a matchup against a 94-win Braves squad fresh off a Wild Card win over the Phillies.
Los Angeles' rest advantage could be significant. Even if he's not pitching, Ohtani has been dealing with lingering injury concerns over the last few months. A week off between his last regular season game should only benefit him, not to mention the Dodgers' ability to line up their loaded starting rotation however they choose. With the Braves using Chris Sale in two games against Philadelphia, he may not be available early in the NLDS.
The Dodgers and Braves have built quite the postseason history. 👀🔥
2013 NLDS — LAD def. ATL
2018 NLDS — LAD def. ATL
2020 NLCS — LAD def. ATL
2021 NLCS — ATL def. LAD
2026 NLDS — ??? 🤔 pic.twitter.com/mHhbDO9gDX
The top of Atlanta's lineup is potent enough to make this an interesting series, and the team did beat the Dodgers five times in the regular season, but Ronald Acuna Jr., Austin Riley and Ozzie Albies will have to meet the moment in the NLDS. Yoshinobu Yamamoto has pitched well against Atlanta in his career, as have Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow.
Even if the Braves' bats can keep things close, it's hard to imagine Atlanta's pitching staff beyond Sale being able to contain Ohtani, Freddie Freeman, Kyle Tucker and Mookie Betts over a five-game series. The Braves are a good team, but the Dodgers are far too talented to fall this early in the bracket.
Prediction: Dodgers in 4
No. 4 San Diego Padres vs. No. 1 Milwaukee Brewers
This matchup pins baseball's best team all season, Milwaukee, against one of its hottest over the past month, San Diego. While the Brewers are the clear favorites here, between the best starting pitcher in the game this season and a deep lineup that plays to contact, the Padres do pose some interesting challenges, going 4-2 against Milwaukee in the regular season.
On one hand, San Diego has stars made for October. As shown in the Wild Card round, when the top of the Padres' lineup is on, they're a hard team to beat — Fernando Tatis Jr., Manny Machado, Xander Boegarts, Ty France and Jackson Merrill can look like one of the best 1-through-5 groups in baseball at times. Add in an elite starter (Michael King) and a strong bullpen led by Mason Miller, and there's a path for the Padres to pull off a stunner here.
Most data has shown that the more of a threat a team is to hit the ball out of the yard, the better they'll fare in the postseason. If this is finally going to be the year the Brewers reach a World Series — putting an end to their cycle of regular season success with playoff shortcomings — they'll need to slug more. This is an offense that's outstanding at making contact and getting on base, but has also continually come up short in October and finished second-to-last in team home runs (154) in the 2026 regular season.
Chances are, Milwaukee won't only be able to rely on its strong pitching staff to reach the World Series. The Brewers' bats will need some extra-base hits. But with the Padres' lackluster starting pitching depth, this is still a series the Brewers can claim even if they're not pristine.
San Diego may have some top-end talent and momentum, but the Padres can't match Milwaukee's all-around depth.
Prediction: Brewers in 4

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Manny Machado Sends Clear Message After Padres' Sweep of Cubs
item.dc:creator: Ricardo Sandoval; Unknown
item.description: San Diego Padres star third baseman Manny Machado is ready for more after sweeping the Chicago Cubs in the wild-card series. Machado and the Padres defeated the Cubs in two games to advance to the National League Division Series. San Diego will now face the top-seeded Milwaukee Brewers in a best-of-five series. item.content:encoded:
San Diego Padres star third baseman Manny Machado is ready for more after sweeping the Chicago Cubs in the wild-card series.
Machado and the Padres defeated the Cubs in two games to advance to the National League Division Series. San Diego will now face the top-seeded Milwaukee Brewers in a best-of-five series.
Although San Diego will be the underdog in this upcoming series, Machado is poised to have three more champagne celebrations in October.
“We’re not done,” Machado said in the postgame locker room celebration. “We’re not done. We’re gonna continue to fight … to bring a championship to the city of San Diego.”
The Padres entered the 2026 postseason as one of the league's hottest teams, and they proved it in two games.
"Man, we've been playing some really good baseball," Machado said. "Hopefully we can keep doing that."
The Padres handled the Cubs in dominant fashion.
Chicago entered the series leading the majors in runs. However, they score just once in 18 innings and mustered only eight hits. The Padres dominated the Cubs in front of their home fans, and the pitching did their part.
Padres ace Michael King started things off with a bang. In Game 1 of the series, King led the way with seven scoreless innings.
Padres starter Nick Pivetta and the bullpen picked up right where King left off on Wednesday night.
"We do have a strong bullpen, and even the guys we haven't used are very good pitchers also," manager Craig Stammen said. "That's going to be the strength of our team as we go through the postseason."
Can the Padres Pull Off an Upset Against the Brewers?
The Padres enter their series against the Brewers as underdogs with +150 odds to come out on top.
The Brewers are major favorites with -180 odds.
Milwaukee enters with the best record in baseball. Likely NL Cy Young winner Jacob Misiorowski leads the Brewers in this series.
The young ace will likely get two starts if the series goes the distance.
While this will certainly be the Padres' toughest test yet, they are as confident as ever to get the job done.
"Momentum’s the biggest thing in baseball," Padres center fielder Jackson Merrill said. "It doesn’t matter whether it’s a regular-season game or a postseason game. Momentum is everything. We know they’re a good baseball team. They play the game to win.
"But you know what? We’re a pretty good baseball team, too."
Sign up for our free newsletter and follow us on Facebook and X/Twitter for the latest news.
Ricardo Sandoval is a freelance writer with On SI. He is a graduate of California State University, Northridge, and specializes in sports writing, particularly in MLB, NBA and NFL. He previously worked with Newsweek and The Sporting News.

item.title: [chicago.suntimes.com] Stinging from playoff exit, Cubs must make sure next year is different: ‘It’s time to look in the mirror’
item.dc:creator: Vinnie Duber
item.description: SAN DIEGO — Was it a successful season in Wrigleyville? It’s hard — even with baseball’s highest scoring lineup, best defense and best player — to judge 2026 as anything but a failure for the Cubs. They set championship-level expectations and World Series goals. Bowing out of the postseason after two games, their offense muzzled and MVP center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong a non-factor, before the calendar even flipped to October? item.content:encoded:
SAN DIEGO — Was it a successful season in Wrigleyville?
It’s hard — even with baseball’s highest scoring lineup, best defense and best player — to judge 2026 as anything but a failure for the Cubs.
They set championship-level expectations and World Series goals.
Bowing out of the postseason after two games, their offense muzzled and MVP center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong a non-factor, before the calendar even flipped to October?
They didn’t come close.
“The goal is to win, and we didn’t play well enough to do that,” third baseman Alex Bregman said. “It’s time to look in the mirror and get better.
“I know myself and a lot of these guys will be thinking about it every day of the offseason and let it fuel us. Just not good enough. We need to get better. In all areas.
“It starts now for everybody in this organization. Assess the year and come back and be better next year, because it wasn’t good enough.”
In the wake of such disappointment, there’s one overarching question: How does this not happen again?
It’s been back-to-back years of this, the Cubs dispatched by the rival Brewers in the NLDS a year ago. That was described as fuel for their fire this season, but the embers didn’t even burn long enough for a rematch.
Craig Counsell, whom the Cubs poached from those Brewers, has two early postseason exits in three seasons at the helm, with two years left on the contract that made him the game’s highest-paid skipper.
“We lost,” Counsell said. “There’s a response to it that we get to choose, and we’ve got to improve. Everybody can point at themselves and say, ‘We’ve got to get a little bit better.’
“We’re going to have to wait to accomplish the thing we really want to accomplish. … We didn’t finish it this year, and you hope that this has to be part of the journey to the ultimate prize.”
With the investments made in Counsell, Bregman, Crow-Armstrong and more, the expectations are not going to change. The Cubs will head into next season thinking World Series, just like this year.
But at least at the moment, they have a lot of questions to answer about how they’re going to get there.
What will make the 2027 group better equipped than the 2026 one?
That’s what the offseason — likely to be halted by a lengthy work stoppage — will teach us.
This was a roller-coaster campaign, with high highs and low lows, a lot of pitching injuries and a final-week downturn that came at exactly the wrong time.
The thoughts on the minds of everyone inside the losing clubhouse Wednesday were of further blows this team is about to take, the players who aren’t going to return, the pending free agents who were such a part of this group and its plan to deliver on those championship-level expectations.
“We’ll talk about the baseball plenty,” second baseman Nico Hoerner said, “but when you get through a locker room with people that you’re really close with and people that aren’t guaranteed to come back here — and not seeing this thing through the way a lot of us envisioned and believed in — that’s the stuff that doesn’t sit right and hurts.”
Perhaps most important for Jed Hoyer’s front office, the Cubs might have to replace their entire starting rotation, with lefties Matthew Boyd, Shota Imanaga and David Peterson, plus righties Clay Holmes and Kevin Gausman, all set to hit free agency.
Righties Cade Horton, Edward Cabrera and Ben Brown, plus lefty Justin Steele, make for an intriguing group of possible replacements, but all are coming off injuries, a risky play.
Then there’s the corner outfielders.
Right fielder Seiya Suzuki has been an offensive force it will be tough for the Cubs to replace; he’s expected to be one of the best hitters on the market and land a big contract.
Left fielder Ian Happ is a franchise fixture whose potential departure had teammates crying Wednesday night.
“He embodies the Cubs more than anyone I know,” shortstop Dansby Swanson said through tears.
Sentimentality is a rare reason to spend for baseball front offices. Happ didn’t have the type of offensive season he consistently has throughout his career though still played excellent defense and hit for power.
“All I can say is that I love being a Cub,” Happ said. “I’ve loved my time. I’ve loved the place, the people, Wrigley Field, the fan base. And it’s been truly special. I don’t think there’s a better place in baseball to play.”
With decisions to make, how Hoyer crafts his roster – and how these Cubs respond to another bout of playoff disappointment – will answer that overarching question, the only question that matters:
How do the Cubs make sure this doesn’t happen again?

item.content:encoded:
In 1969, the San Diego Padres and Milwaukee Brewers — who were the Seattle Pilots for one season — were founded as MLB expansion teams.
Now, 58 short years later, the perennial National League contenders are meeting in the postseason for the first time.
On Saturday, Oct. 3, the best-of-five NLDS will get underway at Milwaukee’s American Family Field with the Brewers’ ace and Cy Young favorite Jacob Misiorowski (16-5, 1.80 ERA) on the hill.
Following a two-game stint in the Cream City, the series will move to SoCal for a pair of contests at San Diego’s PETCO Park. They’re slated to take place:
Game 3
Tuesday, Oct. 6
Game 4
Wednesday, Oct. 7
If you’d like to be there, tickets are available for both high-stakes hypothetical San Diego showdowns.
At the time of publication, the lowest price we could find on tickets for either game was $121 including fees on Vivid Seats.
Prices start at $99 including fees for the three potential meetings in Milwaukee.
Before this series, the Padres got revenge against the Chicago Cubs in the Wild Card round, sweeping MVP hopeful Pete Crow-Armstrong’s club at home after losing to them in three games to open the playoffs last year.
“They’re playing great baseball right now,” San Diego manager Craig Stammen said about his club.
Next up, they have a tall task taking on MLB’s winningest team in 2026.
Oddsmakers project the Brewers are -180 favorites going into the NLDS.
Yet, it should be factored in that San Diego took four of their six meetings over the course of the regular season including a clutch 4-3, eleven-inning victory on Aug. 12.
Is this the year that one of these two clubs finally gets over the hump and returns to the World Series?
While we can’t say for certain we do know that their first-ever postseason meeting with some of the game’s hardest flamethrowers in Misiorowski and Mason Miller should be downright electric.
Don’t miss this one. We just might have an instant classic on our hands.
For more information, our team has everything you need to know and more about the Padres vs. Brewers 2026 NLDS below.

item.content:encoded:
The Atlanta Braves will host the Philadelphia Phillies in a decisive Game Three of the National League Wild Card series tonight (Thursday, October 1). The winner will advance to face the Los Angeles Dodgers in the National League Division Series (NLDS). The Braves won Game One, but the Phillies rallied to win Game Two on Wednesday (September 30), setting the stage for this winner-take-all contest.
The game will start at 8 p.m. ET and will be broadcast on NBC and Peacock. Spanish language coverage will be available on Universo and Univision Radio, while ESPN Radio will provide live national coverage of all 2026 MLB postseason games.
The Phillies' starting pitcher remains undecided, with options including Aaron Nola and ace Zack Wheeler. Meanwhile, the Braves may rely on Grant Holmes to handle the bulk of the innings, though they have not confirmed if he will start or follow an opener. Left-handers Ray Kerr or Brent Suter are potential openers.
Both teams have key players to watch. For the Phillies, Alec Bohm hit a game-winning homer in Game Two, while Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber hit back-to-back homers in the eighth inning to tie the game. On the Braves' side, Michael Harris II and Mauricio Dubón have been performing well at the plate.
The Phillies have a history of postseason success against the Braves, having defeated them in previous playoff series, including the 1993 NLCS and the 2022 and 2023 NLDS. The outcome of tonight's game will determine who advances to face the Dodgers in the next round.

item.content:encoded:
Phillies' Aaron Nola Reportedly Starting vs. Braves over Zack Wheeler For MLB Playoffs Series Finale
The Philadelphia Phillies will go into Thursday's winner-take-all Game 3 against the Atlanta Braves in the National League Wild Card series with Aaron Nola starting on the mound.
Per The Athletic's Matt Gelb, Phillies interim manager Don Mattingly is going with Nola rather than using Zack Wheeler on short rest with a spot in the NLDS at stake.
As a result of their four-game losing streak last week that prevented them from clinching a playoff spot early, the Phillies had to use Wheeler on the final day of the regular season.
Wheeler allowed one run over six innings in a 7-3 win over the Tampa Bay Rays to help Philadelphia secure its postseason berth, but the situation left his status for the wild card round unclear.
Even though Wheeler won't get the start, Mattingly told reporters after Wednesday's 4-3 win to extend the series "it'll be pretty much all hands on deck" for Game 3.
The Phillies are fortunate to have a deep starting staff that allowed them to go with All-Stars Jesús Luzardo and Cristopher Sánchez in the first two games against Atlanta.
However, Game 3 left Mattingly with a decision between Nola or Wheeler. John Clark of NBC Sports Philadelphia noted Wheeler has never started a game in the regular season or playoffs on short rest.
Wheeler's only relief appearance in his MLB career was in Game 7 of the 2023 NLCS against the Arizona Diamondbacks. He tossed 1.2 scoreless innings in a 9-7 loss.
Nola will be pitching on regular rest after starting on Saturday against the Rays. He only made it through one inning, allowing three runs on four hits in a 12-1 loss.
While Nola's overall stat line this season doesn't look great with a 4.67 ERA, he did get better as the year went on. The right-hander had a 3.33 ERA in 14 starts after the All-Star break.
Nola made three starts against Atlanta this season with two coming in a five-day span from Sept. 6-11. He allowed three runs and struck out eight over 13.1 innings in those two outings last month.
The Phillies forced Game 3 against Atlanta thanks to Kyle Schwarber and Bryce Harper hitting back-to-back homers in the eighth to tie the score at three. Alec Bohm delivered the go-ahead solo homer in the top of the 10th.
Andrew Painter finished the game on the mound with three scoreless innings out of the bullpen.
Game 3 between the Phillies and Braves from Truist Park will be played at 8 p.m. ET on Thursday. The winner will advance to play the Los Angeles Dodgers in the NLDS starting on Saturday.

item.content:encoded:
MLB playoff schedule 2026: Full bracket, scores, times, TV channels to watch every postseason series originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
More than seven months after pitchers and catchers reported to spring training, it's time to determine which team will wear the MLB crown in 2026.
Twelve teams reached the postseason bracket, and any discussion about favorites has to start with the two-time defending champion Dodgers. Los Angeles wasn't necessarily dominant during the regular season and enters October with concerns about the health of the planet's best player, Shohei Ohtani, but it has proven unwise to bet against LA lately.
While the Dodgers are in the midst of a dynastic run, neither of the teams that owned the best records in their respective leagues during the regular season — the Brewers and Rays — has won a World Series. Victory would be particularly sweet for either of those fan bases, along with the other postseason entrant without a title, the Padres.
Who will survive the gauntlet to lift the Commissioner's Trophy at the end of October? Here's when and where to watch every game.
Where to watch MLB playoffs 2026
- TV channels: Fox, FS1, TBS, NBC, NBCSN
The 2026 MLB postseason will have a new look for the opening round, with NBC carrying every wild card game on its platforms: NBC, NBCSN and/or Peacock.
After that, the familiar rotation returns. This year's NL playoffs will air on Fox or FS1 while the AL will be on TBS, with the World Series set to air on Fox as it has every year since 2000.
Fans can stream every postseason game except Peacock exclusives with DIRECTV, which offers a free trial to new subscribers.
All games airing on NBC, NBCSN, Fox and FS1 can be streamed with fubo, which also offers a free trial.

item.dc:creator: Billy Heyen
item.description: The Philadelphia Phillies will play in Atlanta against the Braves on Thursday night with their seasons both on the line. It’s a decisive Game 3 of the NL Wild Card Series. The teams split the first two games in the best-of-three series. Only one team can move on. Both teams entered Thursday with a bit of uncertainty about their pitching plans, but things are beginning to take shape. item.content:encoded:
The Philadelphia Phillies will play in Atlanta against the Braves on Thursday night with their seasons both on the line.
It’s a decisive Game 3 of the NL Wild Card Series. The teams split the first two games in the best-of-three series. Only one team can move on.
Both teams entered Thursday with a bit of uncertainty about their pitching plans, but things are beginning to take shape.
According to multiple reports, the Phillies will be starting the veteran Aaron Nola on the mound. It was the most logical decision given that he’s on full rest.
It does raise the question about Zack Wheeler, though. He hasn’t pitched in this series. Would the Phillies really go out of the postseason potentially without even using him?
There’s reason to expect that Wheeler could follow Nola at some point in Thursday’s game.
Is Zack Wheeler Available?
Wheeler is available on Thursday night, according to The Athletic’s Matt Gelb.
“Nola will be on regular rest after pitching most recently in the penultimate game of the regular season Saturday, when he opened a bullpen game on two days’ rest and only threw 21 pitches,” Gelb writes. “The Phillies could also use Zack Wheeler, who is on three days’ rest, as a reliever in Game 3. Jesús Luzardo, who started Game 1 on Tuesday, is in play for an inning or two in Game 3 if needed.”
Wheeler pitched the Phillies’ regular season finale on Sunday against the Tampa Bay Rays. Philadelphia needed to win that game to ensure a playoff spot, and they did, so Wheeler’s arm was used for a good cause there.
Generally, starting pitchers then get at least four days of rest after an outing.
If Wheeler were to pitch Thursday, he would’ve gotten three days of rest — Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday.
Plenty of pitchers go on shorter rest in the playoffs, but it still comes with a risk. It throws off between-start routines and has potentially a greater injury probability.
A pitcher may also be slightly less effective if their arm isn’t feeling as fresh and rested as usual.
Wheeler, though, is one of this era’s great pitchers and had a 3.00 ERA in 28 outings in the regular season for the Phillies. He’s 36 years old now and doesn’t have a ton of time left in his career, most likely. He’d be a logical guy to trust in a big spot on Thursday night.
Of course, if the Phillies were able to win without using Wheeler, he could start Game 1 of the NLDS on Saturday. But that only matters if the Phillies get there.
Zack Wheeler Short Rest History
According to John Clark of NBC Sports Philadelphia, Wheeler has pitched in relief on short rest once in his career.
That was in Game 7 of the 2023 NLCS. The Phillies were eliminated that night, 4-2, by the Diamondbacks.
Wheeler did his part, though. He went 1.2 innings out of the pen, striking out one and walking one while not allowing a hit or a run.

item.title: [New York Daily News] With dad on hand, Cody Bellinger delivers his own big Yankees moment: ‘He’s built for this’
item.dc:creator: Peter Sblendorio
item.description: The night started with Cody Bellinger’s glove. In a sentimental moment before Game 2 of the Wild Card Series, Bellinger caught the ceremonial first pitch from his father, Clay Bellinger, who played for the Yankees from 1999-2001. But by the end of Wednesday night, it was the younger Bellinger’s bat that commanded the attention. Bellinger went 2-for-5 with a home run and four RBI in a 9-2 victory over the Boston Red Sox in the Bronx, completing a lopsided two-game sweep as the Yankees advanced to
item.content:encoded:
The night started with Cody Bellinger’s glove.
In a sentimental moment before Game 2 of the Wild Card Series, Bellinger caught the ceremonial first pitch from his father, Clay Bellinger, who played for the Yankees from 1999-2001.
But by the end of Wednesday night, it was the younger Bellinger’s bat that commanded the attention.
Bellinger went 2-for-5 with a home run and four RBI in a 9-2 victory over the Boston Red Sox in the Bronx, completing a lopsided two-game sweep as the Yankees advanced to the ALDS.
“I’m able to appreciate it in the moment,” Bellinger said afterward, reflecting on sharing the night with his father. “That was a cool moment, just a great game. Happy I was able to contribute, and we’ve got a lot more work to do.”
Continued contributions from Bellinger would go a long way in the Yankees making a deep postseason run, with the AL East-winning Tampa Bay Rays up next in the ALDS.
Bellinger takes on added importance with Aaron Judge sidelined indefinitely due to a calf strain.
He was one of the driving forces in the Yankees’ two-day demolition of the archrival Red Sox, whom they outscored 18-2. The All-Star went 3-for-8 in the series and delivered a pair of key hits in Wednesday’s clincher.
With Yankees leading by a run in the fifth inning, Red Sox manager Chad Tracy controversially removed right-handed starter Sonny Gray after 70 pitches with runners at the corners and two outs.
Tracy turned to the left-handed Erik Miller to face the lefty-swinging Bellinger, who delivered an RBI single that put the Yankees up, 2-0.
Then in the sixth, after an intentional walk to Ben Rice in front of him, Bellinger capped a six-run rally with a three-run home run against right-handed reliever Garrett Whitlock — a 360-foot drive into the right-field stands that served as the dagger.
“He’s built for this,” Judge said Wednesday during a champagne-soaked celebration in the Yankees clubhouse. “He’s built for New York. He’s built for the big moment, and he continues to show up for us when we need him.”
Bellinger, who won the 2019 National League MVP and the 2020 World Series with the Los Angeles Dodgers, is in his second season with the Yankees, having re-signed last winter on a five-year, $162.5 million contract.
Despite missing a month with a hamstring strain, Bellinger batted .264 with 17 home runs, 73 RBI and a .768 OPS in 132 games. He was worth 4.6 WAR (wins above replacement), in part because of his excellent defensive work in left field, too.
“This offseason, there were a couple of other teams involved,” Clay Bellinger said in August of his son’s free agency. “But I said, ‘If you can sign back with these guys, and you go out there and you win a world championship to add to this legacy, there’s no better place in the world to play baseball.’”
The elder Bellinger would know, as the former utility player won World Series with the Yankees in 1999 and 2000.
Now, the Yankees’ World Series aspirations rest in large part with Bellinger, who continues to carve out his own pinstriped legacy.
Despite hitting left-handed, Bellinger is actually better against left-handed pitching than he is against righties, making his bat even more crucial for balance in a Judge-less lineup that’s loaded with lefties.
The Yankees went 15-for-35 (.429) against left-handers in the Red Sox series, with Bellinger recording two hits in those matchups and another top-of-the-order lefty batter in Rice totaling three.
“No secret sauce,” Bellinger said of his reverse splits. “For me, just take it as another at-bat. Felt like when I was playing baseball coming up, didn’t hear too much about the match-ups. I was just playing baseball.”
After hitting .214 in his first postseason with the Yankees, Bellinger is off to a .333 start to this one. Wednesday’s home run was Bellinger’s 11th in the postseason and his second in nine playoff games with the Yankees.
“I feel like I was able to enjoy that one,” Bellinger said. “Just a home game in Yankee Stadium, it’s a really fun atmosphere. It’s fun to play. And hopefully we get many, many more this month.”
