item.title: [Sportsnaut] Red Sox Paid a Massive Price for Adley Rutschman to Win in October. Then They Went 0-2
item.dc:creator: Gary Adornato
item.description: Boston was already headed toward the playoffs when it surrendered four prospects and its starting catcher for Rutschman. The Yankees reportedly rejected Baltimore’s asking price — then swept the Red Sox out of October. Let’s be clear about why the Boston Red Sox acquired Adley Rutschman. They didn’t need him to save their season. They didn’t need him to drag them into postseason contention. And they certainly didn’t surrender four prospects and their starting major-league catcher simply to hang
item.content:encoded:
Boston was already headed toward the playoffs when it surrendered four prospects and its starting catcher for Rutschman. The Yankees reportedly rejected Baltimore’s asking price — then swept the Red Sox out of October.
Let’s be clear about why the Boston Red Sox acquired Adley Rutschman.
They didn’t need him to save their season.
They didn’t need him to drag them into postseason contention.
And they certainly didn’t surrender four prospects and their starting major-league catcher simply to hang a Wild Card banner.
Boston was already one of baseball’s hottest teams when it acquired Rutschman from the Baltimore Orioles at the Aug. 3 trade deadline. The Red Sox had transformed their season with a remarkable summer surge and were firmly positioned to reach the postseason.
Rutschman was supposed to provide something more.
October.
The Red Sox paid an enormous price to a division rival because they believed adding a three-time All-Star catcher could help turn a playoff team into a championship team.
Instead, their postseason lasted two games.
The New York Yankees completed an embarrassing two-game sweep Wednesday night, beating Boston 9-2 after a 9-0 demolition in Game 1.
Final aggregate score: Yankees 18, Red Sox 2.
Boston managed only seven hits in 18 innings and batted .117 in the series. The Yankees did all of it without three-time American League MVP Aaron Judge, who was sidelined by a calf injury.
And Rutschman?
The expensive deadline addition Boston acquired specifically to make a difference at this time of year couldn’t make one.
Making matters considerably worse, the Yankees reportedly had their own opportunity to acquire Rutschman.
They decided Baltimore’s price was too high.
Then they sent Boston home.
Boston Didn’t Need Adley Rutschman to Reach the Playoffs
This is the most important context when evaluating the trade.
The Red Sox weren’t desperately chasing the final Wild Card position when chief baseball officer Craig Breslow made the deal.
Boston had gone 23-3 beginning July 2, establishing itself as one of baseball’s hottest teams and putting itself firmly on a postseason trajectory before Rutschman ever put on a Red Sox uniform.
That’s why simply pointing out that Boston reached the postseason after acquiring him misses the point.
Reaching October wasn’t supposed to justify the trade.
Winning in October was.
The Red Sox ultimately finished 87-75 and secured a Wild Card berth. Then the Yankees eliminated them in two games.
So what exactly did Boston’s massive deadline investment change?
Not its playoff destination and certainly not its playoff result.
Adley Rutschman Didn’t Deliver When Boston Needed Him Most
This was the stage for which Boston acquired Rutschman.
Instead, the Red Sox scored two runs in two games.
Rutschman finished the series 1-for-8 with three strikeouts and did not drive in a run as Boston’s offense was overwhelmed by Cam Schlittler and Max Fried.
And one of his most consequential moments came defensively during Boston’s disastrous sixth inning Wednesday.
With the Red Sox trailing 2-1 and desperately trying to keep their season alive, Spencer Jones reached first after swinging at a third strike from Garrett Crochet that got away from Rutschman.
Jones then stole second and advanced to third when Rutschman’s throw sailed into center field.
George Lombard Jr. followed with an RBI single.
The inning disintegrated from there.
By the time Boston finally recorded the third out, New York had scored six runs and transformed a one-run elimination game into another rout.
It would be ridiculous to blame Rutschman for Boston’s elimination. The Red Sox were comprehensively outplayed, their offense disappeared and their pitching couldn’t contain New York when the series was on the line.
But that’s precisely why the trade deserves scrutiny.
Boston didn’t surrender a collection of valuable young players for another complementary piece.
It paid for a difference-maker.
When the difference needed to be made, it wasn’t.
Look at What Boston Gave Baltimore
The price looks even more jarring now.
Baltimore received five players:
RHP Anthony Eyanson: Boston’s No. 2 prospect at the time of the trade and a top-50 prospect in baseball. He immediately became Baltimore’s top-ranked prospect.
RHP Kyson Witherspoon: Another highly regarded pitching prospect who immediately became one of the better prospects in Baltimore’s system.
OF Enddy Azocar: A promising young outfielder who added another high-upside asset to Baltimore’s farm system.
C Carlos Narváez: Boston’s starting major-league catcher, giving Baltimore an immediate replacement behind the plate.
OF Harold Rivas: The 18-year-old outfielder eventually sent to Baltimore as the player to be named later.
Boston received Rutschman, catcher Jake Rogers and cash.
Four prospects and a starting major-league catcher.
Sent directly to an American League East rival.
That’s not a routine deadline upgrade.
That’s a significant transfer of organizational value made specifically because Boston believed Rutschman could help it win immediately.
The immediate payoff?
Thirty-two regular-season games and a postseason that lasted two losses.
The Yankees Were Offered Adley Rutschman, Too. They Walked Away.
This is where Boston’s decision becomes even harder to swallow.
The Red Sox weren’t the only AL East contender that discussed Rutschman with Baltimore.
The Yankees reportedly explored acquiring him before the deadline.
According to the New York Post, Baltimore’s asking price from New York included pitching prospect Elmer Rodríguez, catcher Austin Wells, outfield prospect Yostin Pena and either Will Warren or Ryan Weathers.
The Yankees decided it was too much.
Boston decided its own massive prospect package wasn’t.
Two months later, the teams met in October.
The Yankees swept the Red Sox.
That alone doesn’t prove New York made the correct long-term decision. Prospects fail. Rutschman could return to All-Star form. The careers of the players Boston and New York retained or surrendered will ultimately determine how these decisions age.
But the immediate comparison couldn’t be much uglier for Breslow.
New York kept its catcher.
It kept its prospects.
It kept its young pitching.
And it eliminated the team that paid Baltimore’s price.
Ben Rice Made the Comparison Even More Painful
There is another piece of this that Boston probably doesn’t want to think about.
The Yankees didn’t merely decline to acquire Rutschman.
They watched one of their own young players become the kind of offensive weapon Boston hoped it was acquiring.
Ben Rice erupted for 41 home runs during the regular season.
Then he opened the postseason by destroying the Red Sox.
Rice went 4-for-5 with two home runs and six RBIs in New York’s 9-0 Game 1 victory.
Six RBIs.
Boston scored two runs in the entire series.
The Yankees didn’t need to surrender a massive package to Baltimore to find an impact bat.
They developed one.
Boston went shopping for an established star.
Then Rice helped send its expensive new catcher and the rest of the Red Sox home.
Boston Didn’t Even Get the Superstar Version of Rutschman
Boston can at least point to Rutschman’s impressive résumé.
He was the No. 1 overall pick in the 2019 MLB Draft, became the centerpiece of Baltimore’s rebuild and developed into one of baseball’s most recognizable catchers.
But the Red Sox weren’t trading for his résumé.
They were trading for what he could do in 2026 and 2027.
That’s an important distinction.
Rutschman was already on the injured list with wrist inflammation when Boston acquired him.
Once healthy, he played 32 regular-season games for the Red Sox and hit .222 with a .278 on-base percentage and .410 slugging percentage.
His OPS was .688.
He hit five home runs and drove in 13 runs.
His 92 OPS+ meant he was eight percent below league average offensively after adjusting for league and ballpark conditions.
Boston surrendered four prospects and its starting catcher for an immediate upgrade and received below-average regular-season offense.
Then came October.
No transformational performance.
No postseason victory.
No series win.
Craig Breslow Made a Win-Now Trade. Boston Didn’t Win.
There is nothing inherently wrong with trading prospects.
Contending organizations sometimes become too protective of players who have never taken a major-league at-bat. Windows close. Players get hurt. Rosters change.
When an organization has an opportunity to win a championship, there are times when being aggressive is exactly the right approach.
But here’s the other side of that philosophy:
If you’re going to make a win-now trade, eventually you have to win now.
Breslow pushed a significant portion of Boston’s prospect capital into the middle of the table.
The Red Sox responded by finishing 87-75.
Then they arrived at Yankee Stadium and were outscored 18-2 in two games.
That’s not an October run.
That’s barely an October appearance.
The Yankees advanced. Boston went home before October was two days old.
And the player Breslow acquired as his blockbuster deadline upgrade produced neither the offensive impact nor the postseason difference Boston was paying for.
Meanwhile, Baltimore Gets to Keep All Five Players
This is the part that could hurt Boston considerably longer than Wednesday night’s loss.
Baltimore doesn’t need all four prospects to become stars for this trade to sting the Red Sox.
It doesn’t even need two of them to become stars.
If Eyanson develops into a quality major-league starter, or Witherspoon reaches his upside, or Azocar or Rivas eventually develops into an everyday player, Boston could spend years watching a division rival benefit from its deadline gamble.
Narváez is already a major-league catcher.
The Orioles essentially converted one player approaching his final season of club control into five assets.
Boston acquired the short-term star.
Baltimore acquired years of potential value.
And the Orioles didn’t have to wait long to see the first part of their gamble work.
Rutschman’s first postseason with Boston lasted two games.
Now Boston May Have to Pay for Rutschman Again
That’s what makes this more than simply a failed 2026 deadline gamble.
Rutschman can become a free agent after the 2027 season.
Boston therefore has another major decision coming.
The Red Sox can attempt to sign him to a lucrative extension, committing significant long-term money to a catcher whose offensive production has declined from his early-career peak and who has dealt with injuries.
They can let him play out 2027 and risk watching him depart as a free agent roughly 17 months after surrendering four prospects and Narváez to acquire him.
Or they can eventually trade him and attempt to recover some of the organizational value they sent Baltimore.
None looks particularly attractive this morning.
And Boston should be especially careful about allowing the enormous acquisition cost to influence its next decision.
The prospects are gone regardless.
Paying Rutschman a huge extension because Boston already paid dearly to acquire him would be classic sunk-cost thinking.
The next decision has to be based on what Rutschman is likely to provide going forward, not what Boston surrendered to get him.
He could make this entire discussion look foolish next season. Rutschman is talented enough to rebound, produce another All-Star season and become an important part of a championship contender.
But that’s a 2027 argument.
We know what happened in 2026.
Boston was already headed toward the postseason.
Baltimore put an enormous price on Rutschman.
The Yankees looked at that price and walked away.
The Red Sox paid it.
Then those two teams met in October.
New York outscored Boston 18-2, swept the Red Sox in two games and advanced without Aaron Judge.
Boston went home.
And Baltimore still has all five players.

item.title: [MLB.com] Phillies vs. Braves NL Wild Card Series Game 3 FAQ (8 ET, NBC/Peacock)
item.dc:creator: Mark Bowman; Todd Zolecki; Paul Casella
item.description: In a series that is shaping up to be another instant classic between the bitter NL East rivals, it now all comes down to Game 3 on Thursday. A Phillies win would set up an NLDS rematch from last year against the Dodgers, while the Braves hope to punch their ticket to the NLDS for the first time since 2023. “Just win a game,” said Phillies infielder Alec Bohm, who hit the game-winning homer in the Phillies’ 4-3 extra-inning victory in Game 2. “ … I think as much as we want to enjoy this for a lit
item.content:encoded:
In a series that is shaping up to be another instant classic between the bitter NL East rivals, it now all comes down to Game 3 on Thursday. A Phillies win would set up an NLDS rematch from last year against the Dodgers, while the Braves hope to punch their ticket to the NLDS for the first time since 2023.
“Just win a game,” said Phillies infielder Alec Bohm, who hit the game-winning homer in the Phillies’ 4-3 extra-inning victory in Game 2. “ … I think as much as we want to enjoy this for a little bit, it's the same as we did [after Game 1]: Turn the page, and move on to tomorrow and show up ready to do the same thing.”
So, what could the Phillies and Braves possibly have in store for their winner-take-all showdown?
While that’s the biggest question looming over the National League Wild Card Series, it’s far from the only one. Here’s everything you need to know about Game 3:
When is the game and how can I watch it?
The game will begin at 8 p.m. ET and air on NBC and Peacock.
The Wild Card Series will be available in Spanish on Universo, while Univision Radio will provide Spanish language audio coverage. ESPN Radio will provide live national coverage of all 2026 MLB postseason games, beginning with the Wild Card Series.
Who are the starting pitchers?
Phillies: TBD
The Phillies planned to meet following Game 2 to discuss their pitching plans for this week’s third elimination game. Phillies interim manager Don Mattingly said Monday that Aaron Nola was setting up to start Game 3, but there’s no question things can change. It wouldn’t be a surprise to see ace Zack Wheeler start on short rest. If he doesn’t start, there’s no doubt he’d enter the game in relief.
Braves: TBD
Grant Holmes will attempt to handle the bulk of the innings. But the Braves haven’t said whether he’ll start or possibly follow an opener. The top options to open are left-handers Ray Kerr or Brent Suter. Either would be tasked with handling Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber in the first inning.
What might the starting lineups look like?
Braves: The Braves’ lineup appears much more formidable against right-handed pitchers. With Mike Yastrzemski in left field, Mauricio Dubón would move to shortstop, which was where Ha-Seong Kim started during the first two games.
How will the bullpens line up after the starter?
Phillies: Mattingly said it’s “all hands on deck,” although closer Jhoan Duran wasn’t available in Game 2. Mattingly said he hoped he’d have Duran in Game 3. But other than Cristopher Sánchez, who started Game 2, probably every pitcher on the Phillies’ staff will be available in some capacity in Game 3. That’s everybody from Wheeler to Luzardo to Painter.
Braves: Closer Raisel Iglesias and his top setup men Didier Fuentes and Dylan Lee both pitched in the first two games of this series. Each should be available in this winner-take-all game. Robert Suarez hasn’t been utilized yet. He missed three months with an elbow ailment before making two appearances last week. But manager Walt Weiss may have no other choice but to turn to the right-hander, who posted a 0.56 ERA in 31 appearances before his elbow became a problem in June.
Any injuries of note?
Braves: OF Lane Thomas could be available during the NLDS. Starting pitchers Bryce Elder (arthroscopic knee surgery), Reynaldo López (right shoulder inflammation) and Martín Pérez (lower back discomfort) may also be available in future rounds.
Who is hot and who is not?
Phillies: Home runs often come in bunches for Schwarber and Harper. Did their back-to-back homers in the eighth inning in Game 2 get them going? Bohm is 3-for-8 with one double and one home run in the series. After struggling all season, Realmuto has two hits and two RBIs this series.
Anything else fans might want to know?
The Phillies are 1-3 in franchise history in win-or-go-home postseason games. They won Game 5 of the 1980 NLCS. They lost Game 7 of the 2023 NLCS, Game 5 of the 2011 NLDS and Game 5 of the 1981 NLDS.

item.title: [foxwilmington.com] Phillies force Game 3 as Kyle Schwarber, Bryce Harper go back-to-back and Alec Bohm homers in 10th vs Braves
item.dc:creator: FOX Wilmington

His two-out homer in the 10th inning lifted the Phillies to a 4-3 victory over the Atlanta Braves and forced a winner-take-all Game 3. The Phillies had trailed 3-1 before Kyle Schwarber and Bryce Harper hit back-to-back homers in the seventh. Harper’s blast came one inning after he committed a costly fielding error. item.content:encoded:
Game 2 of the National League Wild Card Series was deadlocked at 3-3 Wednesday afternoon before Alec Bohm delivered Philadelphia’s biggest swing. His two-out homer in the 10th inning lifted the Phillies to a 4-3 victory over the Atlanta Braves and forced a winner-take-all Game 3.
The Phillies had trailed 3-1 before Kyle Schwarber and Bryce Harper hit back-to-back homers in the seventh. Harper’s blast came one inning after he committed a costly fielding error.
This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.
Andrew Painter then took over. The regular-season starter worked three scoreless innings to protect Philadelphia’s taxed bullpen, stranded two runners in the 10th and struck out Dominic Smith after the Phillies won an ABS challenge.
Playing under traditional extra-inning rules that don’t include designated runners at second base like in the regular season, Bohm delivered his third career postseason home run, a 357-foot shot to right field off right-hander Didier Fuentes.
The Phillies will try to continue their postseason dominance over the Braves in Thursday’s Game 3. Philadelphia beat Atlanta in the 1993 NLCS and the 2022 and 2023 NLDS.
In the seventh, Drake Baldwin’s double glanced off Harper’s glove in right field, driving in Sean Murphy to give Atlanta a 2-1 lead. Harper, who resumed playing the outfield late this season for the first time since 2022, got a poor jump and was leaping for the ball near the warning track. He was not charged with an error. Matt Olson added a sacrifice fly.
“Probably should have been caught, obviously,” Harper said.
The Phillies pulled even with eighth-inning home runs by Schwarber and Harper off Dylan Lee, the winning pitcher in the Braves‘ 5-3 opening win on Tuesday. Schwarber’s drive carried 447 feet and Harper followed with a 418-foot drive.
Tyler Mahle allowed one run on six hits in seven innings for Atlanta. Cristopher Sánchez allowed three runs in 6 2/3 innings for Philadelphia while throwing a career-high 116 pitches.

Tyler Mahle allowed one run on six hits in seven innings for Atlanta. Cristopher Sánchez allowed three runs in 6.2 innings for Philadelphia while throwing a career-high 116 pitches.
The start time for the decisive Game 3 has not yet been determined. The Braves announced that MLB will schedule the game for either 2:15 p.m. ET or 8:15 p.m. ET in Atlanta, with the final time dependent on the conclusion of the other three Wild Card Series Game 2 matchups tonight.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: [MLB.com] Bullpen stung by long ball after Mahle's strong playoff debut
item.dc:creator: Mark Bowman
item.description: ATLANTA -- Six outs away from finally killing Philadelphia’s hex, the Braves were undone by their bullpen, the portion of their roster that was supposed to be a postseason strength. “I was at shortstop when Kirk Gibson did his thing off one of the greatest closers of all time,” Braves manager Walt Weiss said. “It comes with the territory when you're pitching late in close games. Every once in a while, they get you.” Nearly 40 years later, Weiss still remembers the sting he and his A’s teammates
item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA -- Six outs away from finally killing Philadelphia’s hex, the Braves were undone by their bullpen, the portion of their roster that was supposed to be a postseason strength.
“I was at shortstop when Kirk Gibson did his thing off one of the greatest closers of all time,” Braves manager Walt Weiss said. “It comes with the territory when you're pitching late in close games. Every once in a while, they get you.”
Nearly 40 years later, Weiss still remembers the sting he and his A’s teammates felt when an injured Gibson came off the bench to hit a walk-off homer against Hall of Fame closer Dennis Eckersley in Game 1 of the 1988 World Series at Dodger Stadium.
A similar type of sting was felt as the Braves blew a two-run eighth-inning lead in a 4-3, 10-inning loss to the Phillies in Game 2 of the NL Wild Card Series on Wednesday afternoon at Truist Park. Dylan Lee surrendered consecutive homers to Kyle Schwarber and Bryce Harper in the eighth. Didier Fuentes allowed Alec Bohm’s decisive homer with two outs in the 10th.
“That's life,” Braves starting pitcher Tyler Mahle said. “Sometimes, it happens. There's nothing really else to say about it. It sucks now, but we're going to have a chance to go out there tomorrow and turn it around.”
Now, Weiss’ bunch must win Game 3 on Thursday to avoid being eliminated from the playoffs by Philadelphia for the fourth time overall and third time in the past five years. The Phillies eliminated Atlanta teams that won 100-plus regular-season games in 1993 (NLCS), 2022 (NLDS) and 2023 (NLDS).
Thursday's Game 3, airing on NBC and Peacock, will start at 8 p.m. ET.
“[The Braves] have played great at home,” Harper said. “But again, I'll just talk about the postseason; it's just a different animal.”
Mahle proved he was up to the challenge during what was his first postseason appearance. The right-hander, acquired from the Giants on Aug. 2, became the first Braves pitcher to allow one run or none over seven-plus innings in the postseason since Max Fried threw seven scoreless against the Reds in Game 1 of the 2020 NL Wild Card Series.
Once Harper misplayed a Drake Baldwin fly ball into a go-ahead double off Phillies starter Cristopher Sánchez during Atlanta’s two-run seventh, it looked like the Braves were destined for a great storyline.
But instead of celebrating how their trade acquisition helped them end the Phillies’ playoff dominance, the Braves were reminded that Lee hasn’t been nearly as good as he was before the All-Star break, when he posted a 1.47 ERA in 43 innings (44 appearances).
When Schwarber opened the eighth with a Statcast-projected 447-foot homer and Harper followed by depositing another ball into the right-field seats, Lee extended the troubles he had while posting a 6.00 ERA in 24 innings after the break. It should be noted he allowed just two homers during that stretch, and he did not allow any home runs to left-handed batters during the regular season.
“Lee’s our high-leverage lefty,” Weiss said. “He put down the same part of the order yesterday.”
Lee struck out Schwarber and got Harper to fly out in Game 1. How might he fare if he’s asked to go through these left-handed sluggers for a third straight day?
How about Fuentes? The rookie right-hander was masterful during the regular season, posting a 2.05 ERA in 70 1/3 innings as a reliever. But he surrendered J.T. Realmuto’s two-run triple in Game 1, and his psyche was bruised again Wednesday when Bohm sneaked his game-winning homer over the right-field wall.
“[Fuentes] made a good pitch,” Baldwin said. “I think if we need him tomorrow, he'll be ready to go, and I don't think he'll let that affect him too much.”
The Phillies’ rotation was a concern entering this series because Zack Wheeler was needed to pitch on Sunday with a postseason spot on the line. Well, Aaron Nola and Wheeler could be used in Game 3.
As for the Braves, they haven’t announced who will start Game 3. Grant Holmes will be lined up to pitch at least four innings. But will he start? Or will either Ray Kerr or Brent Suter take the mound as an opener?
More importantly, can the Braves bounce back from this and finally end their playoff struggles against their division rivals?

item.title: [MLB.com] 'Never a doubt': Resilient Phils force Game 3 on three dramatic swings
item.dc:creator: Todd Zolecki
item.description: He removed his cap and sat in a crouch with two outs in the seventh inning on Wednesday afternoon at Truist Park. Phillies interim manager Don Mattingly had just walked to the mound to remove Cristopher Sánchez from the game, two batters after Harper’s misplay on a fly ball to right sparked Atlanta’s go-ahead two-run rally in Game 2 of the NL Wild Card Series. item.content:encoded:
He removed his cap and sat in a crouch with two outs in the seventh inning on Wednesday afternoon at Truist Park. Phillies interim manager Don Mattingly had just walked to the mound to remove Cristopher Sánchez from the game, two batters after Harper’s misplay on a fly ball to right sparked Atlanta’s go-ahead two-run rally in Game 2 of the NL Wild Card Series. Guns N’ Roses blasted throughout the ballpark as the Braves reveled in Harper’s misfortune.
“Obviously a world of emotion there,” Harper said. “I'll tell you what. I was thinking about Krew, my son, what I would say to him in that situation.”
The Phillies were six outs from another crushing season-ending loss and perhaps significant offseason changes. But then the unbelievable happened. The Phillies won in 10 innings, 4-3. Kyle Schwarber and Harper hit back-to-back homers in the eighth inning to tie it. Alec Bohm hit an opposite-field homer in the 10th to take the lead. Rookie Andrew Painter pitched three scoreless innings of relief in the first postseason performance of his career.
“What a sport,” Harper said.
“A great gift,” said Jesús Luzardo, celebrating his 29th birthday.
“It’s in our DNA,” Schwarber said. “We’re just not going to quit.”
Thursday's Game 3, airing on NBC and Peacock, will start at 8 p.m. ET.
Sánchez allowed a leadoff walk in the seventh inning to Sean Murphy. Ha-Seong Kim bunted a ball toward the mound. Bohm, who turned a fantastic 3-2-3 double play to end the sixth, inexplicably tried to get the lead runner at second base. He did not.
Two batters later, Harper misjudged Drake Baldwin’s fly ball to right. It tipped over the top of his glove to allow a run to score.
Sánchez found Harper in the dugout afterward.
“I told him that he was bound to have a great moment,” Sánchez said via team interpreter Diego D’Aniello.
“I just tapped him on the butt and said, ‘You’ve got this,’” J.T. Realmuto said.
Schwarber started the inning against Braves left-hander Dylan Lee, who hadn’t allowed a homer to a left-hander in 92 at-bats this season. He hit a 3-2 slider a Statcast-projected 447 feet. Braves right fielder Ronald Acuña Jr. didn’t even bother to turn around to watch the ball leave the ballpark.
Harper greeted Schwarber at home plate.
“Hey, man, just try to find a way on,” Schwarber told Harper.
Instead, Harper smashed a 1-1 slider to right field to tie the game.
“I wasn't not trying to hit a homer, I can tell you that,” Harper said. “For me, everybody is going to make mistakes at some point, but it's how you come through in the next situation.
“It's not that serious, to tell you the truth. I think people take it very seriously -- and don't get me wrong, I take it serious. But I think there's a mindset, especially for kids nowadays, is parents and coaches put so much on kids these days to have to come through and be great. But for me, it's, 'How can you learn from each situation that you're in to come out great in the next one?'”
It was one of the more dramatic moments in Phillies postseason history considering how everything had unfolded in the bottom of the seventh inning, with the Phillies’ season and future of the organization on the line.
“What just happened,” reliever Tim Mayza said.
“That wasn’t stressful at all,” Zack Wheeler said.
Painter put up zeros to give the Phillies a chance to win it in the 10th.
“That’s a career-altering performance in my opinion,” Realmuto said.
Bohm hit the go-ahead homer in the 10th against Didier Fuentes.
“I didn't know it was gone until I heard it hit -- kind of rattle against the fence above the wall,” Bohm said.
It was Bohm’s first opposite-field home run since Opening Day. Bohm became the fourth player in Phillies history to hit a go-ahead homer in extra innings of a postseason game, joining George Vukovich (1981 NLDS Game 4), Lenny Dykstra (1993 NLDS Game 5) and Realmuto (2022 World Series Game 1).
“I've seen some great ones that this has happened to,” Braves manager Walt Weiss said. “I saw one of the greatest. I was at shortstop when Kirk Gibson did his thing off one of the greatest closers [Dennis Eckersley] of all time [in Game 1 of the 1988 World Series]. It comes with the territory when you're pitching late in close games. Every once in a while, they get you.”
But it’s not over yet. The Phillies need to win Thursday to keep their season alive. They are 1-3 in franchise history in win-or-go-home postseason games. They won Game 5 of the 1980 NLCS. They lost Game 7 of the 2023 NLCS, Game 5 of the 2011 NLDS and Game 5 of the 1981 NLDS.
“We have to keep going,” Schwarber said.
Painter struck out Dominic Smith looking on an 0-2 fastball -- after an appropriately dramatic and successful challenge by Realmuto, the first game-ending ABS challenge in postseason history -- to end the game at 5:19 p.m. ET. Trea Turner, who went 1-for-5 with a double, returned to the Phillies’ clubhouse by himself 32 minutes later.
He had just left the batting cage near the visitors’ dugout. He carried two bats in each hand.
He had been working, preparing for Game 3.
“Never a doubt,” Turner said about the win.

item.title: [newstribune.com] White Sox sweep Astros for first postseason series win since 2005 | Jefferson City News-Tribune
item.dc:creator: MK Bower; Field Level Media
item.description: HOUSTON -- Chase Meidroth hit a backbreaking three-run home run in the sixth inning to help the Chicago White Sox make a big early lead stand up in a 7-3 victory Wednesday against the Houston Astros that capped a two-game sweep of their American League wild-card series. The White Sox earned their first postseason series victory since their sweep of the Astros in the 2005 World Series. The White Sox will face the Cleveland Guardians in a best-of-5 American League Division Series that begins Satur
item.content:encoded:
HOUSTON -- Chase Meidroth hit a backbreaking three-run home run in the sixth inning to help the Chicago White Sox make a big early lead stand up in a 7-3 victory Wednesday against the Houston Astros that capped a two-game sweep of their American League wild-card series.
The White Sox earned their first postseason series victory since their sweep of the Astros in the 2005 World Series. The White Sox will face the Cleveland Guardians in a best-of-5 American League Division Series that begins Saturday in Cleveland.
“I’m really just happy for everybody over the last few years who experienced White Sox baseball when it obviously wasn’t at its best,” Chicago manager Will Venable said postgame. “It’s such a storied franchise. (White Sox owner) Jerry (Reinsdorf) put so much into this team, loves this team so much, and to be able to reward him and the city of Chicago, who have been in our corner and supported us from Day 1 that I’ve been there, just feels really good.
“I’m proud of the guys and certainly happy for them. They’re probably the only ones in this country that believed they could be in this spot, and they maintained that belief in the beginning of the season and went throughout the season maintaining that. They made it happen.”
The Astros returned to the playoffs after a one-year absence but have not advanced past the wild-card round since 2023.
“(Astros owner) Jim (Crane) has been very clear about his process and when he wants to have that conversation,” Houston manager Joe Espada, who finishes the season without an extension in place to stay with the Astros. “I respect the process and how blessed I’ve been to have been here for over nine years, experienced so many division titles, championship series, World Series -- winning one as a bench coach. As a manager, I have witnessed so many great moments. Obviously, I would like to continue enjoying those moments.”
After the Astros left the bases loaded in the fifth, Meidroth extended a 4-3 lead by driving a 3-1 slider from Astros reliever Bryan Abreu 390 feet to left-center field.
The White Sox scored four runs in the top of the first inning off Astros ace Hunter Brown (0-1), who didn’t make it out of the first as he allowed five hits, four runs (three earned) and one walk while the defense contributed two errors.
Kyle Teel, Andrew Benintendi and Tristan Peters recorded RBI singles in the first while Miguel Vargas reached on a fielding error by Astros third baseman Nick Allen and scored on a throwing error by center fielder Lucas Spence. Brown retired two of the nine batters he faced.
The Astros began a methodical climb back into the game in the bottom of the first when leadoff man Jeremy Pena smacked the first of three solo home runs off Chicago starter Sean Burke.
Pena drilled a 1-1 slider 395 feet to left-center field. An inning later, Cam Smith bashed a 1-0 sinker 440 feet to left field to close the margin to 4-2. In the fourth inning, Jose Altuve socked his 28th career postseason homer -- second all-time to Manny Ramirez -- to left to bring Houston within 4-3.
Burke allowed three runs and four hits while recording eight strikeouts in four innings. When the Astros built another serious threat in the fifth, White Sox left-hander Anthony Kay delivered.
After reliever Huascar Brazoban hit Cam Smith with a pitch and gave up a single to Pena, Kay (1-0) entered with one out and retired MVP candidate Yordan Alvarez on a deep fly just in front of the Crawford Boxes in left. Kay loaded the bases by walking Isaac Paredes but induced Altuve into a harmless flyout to right to end the inning.
Peter Lambert, the Astros’ third pitcher of the game, needed only 36 pitches to work three perfect innings, but he walked Benintendi and Peters to open the sixth. After Abreu entered the game, Meidroth faked a bunt that enabled pinch runner Luisangel Acuna and Peters to steal third and second base, respectively. With the infield in, Meidroth made it moot by crushing a hanging slider he immediately knew was a home run.

item.content:encoded:
Major League Baseball announced today that it has approved a roster substitution for the Boston Red Sox due to an injury sustained by outfielder Roman Anthony. As a result, Anthony will be replaced by Curtis Mead on Boston’s roster vs. New York Yankees in the American League Wild Card Series presented by AbbVie. Dr. Gary Green, MLB’s Medical Director, confirmed the injury after a full review of the medical information.
MLB Postseason rules provide that a Club may request permission from the Commissioner’s Office to replace a player who is unable to play because of an injury. The Commissioner’s Office may approve or disapprove the request based on the specific facts and circumstances. In accordance with the rules, Anthony will be ineligible to return in the American League Division Series presented by Booking.com if the Red Sox participate, but he would be eligible to return for the American League Championship Series if Boston qualifies.
The Wild Card Series presented by AbbVie will be broadcast by NBC, Peacock and NBC Sports Network while ESPN Radio provides live national coverage. MLB Network will air extensive studio coverage throughout the Postseason across the Emmy Award-winning MLB Tonight, the Emmy-nominated MLB Central and MLB Now, and Intentional Talk, MLB Network’s longest-running talk show. Postseason games throughout 2026 will also be telecast in Spanish on Universo and Univision, while Univision Radio will provide Spanish language audio coverage. The 2026 Postseason will be distributed by MLB media rightsholders in 16 different languages to fans in more than 200 countries and territories.

item.content:encoded:
Major League Baseball announced the broadcast schedule for the 2026 Wild Card Series presented by AbbVie. The 2026 postseason will begin with each of the four Wild Card Series scheduled from Tuesday through Thursday under a best-of-three format, all available across NBC Sports platforms, including NBC, Peacock and NBC Sports Network. Coverage of the Wild Card Series marks the return of postseason baseball to NBC for the first time since the 2000 ALCS.
The Wild Card Series will be available in Spanish on Universo, while Univision Radio will provide Spanish language audio coverage. ESPN Radio will provide live national coverage of all 2026 MLB postseason games, beginning with the Wild Card Series. In addition, MLB Network will air extensive studio coverage throughout the postseason across the Emmy Award-winning MLB Tonight, the Emmy-nominated MLB Central and MLB Now, and Intentional Talk, MLB Network’s longest-running talk show.

item.title: [MLB.com] Pivetta tabbed to start Game 2 after missing most of 2026 with right elbow injury
item.dc:creator: Cole Bradley
item.description: SAN DIEGO -- Through Nick Pivetta’s first four starts this season, it was clear he was picking up right where he left off from his career-best 2025 campaign, one that saw him finish sixth in National League Cy Young Award voting … only for it to be derailed by a right elbow injury in April that cost him nearly five months. item.content:encoded:
SAN DIEGO -- Through Nick Pivetta’s first four starts this season, it was clear he was picking up right where he left off from his career-best 2025 campaign, one that saw him finish sixth in National League Cy Young Award voting … only for it to be derailed by a right elbow injury in April that cost him nearly five months.
But upon his return on Sept. 7, Pivetta reassumed the version of himself that was prevalent throughout last year, putting a lengthy rehab behind him and leaving no doubt that he was fully ready to contribute on the biggest stage.
This time, though, he’ll have the Petco Park crowd behind him.
“We're very lucky to have such a great fan base here,” Pivetta said. “From what I've heard from the guys that have played here before, I'm expecting great things and very excited for it. Just trying to keep all my focus on the game, but enjoy those moments, too, with those fans and try to bring the championship home for them.”
Since returning from the injured list, Pivetta has looked a lot like the guy who posted a 2.87 ERA across 31 starts in ‘25. He allowed a mere three runs over 18 2/3 innings over four starts, good for a 1.45 ERA. He delivered 4 2/3 scoreless frames against the Dodgers in Los Angeles his last time out, helping the Padres secure their third consecutive trip to the postseason that night.
“High level of confidence with Nick, what a road he’s been on this year,” Padres manager Craig Stammen said. “For him, when it didn’t look great at the beginning of the season, to put in the work over an entire season and not know if he’s ever going to get back … now he’s [been] one of our best pitchers down the stretch.”
The four-start runway Pivetta had allowed him to build up to full pitch count (he threw 87 pitches in his last start), meaning there should be zero limitations for him this postseason.
Of course, the Padres almost certainly won’t need him to go a full four or five innings, given their elite bullpen that was pieced together specifically to help shorten games in the playoffs -- a formula that San Diego has deployed with great success in its previous seasons and seems poised to do once more.
But Pivetta’s postseason track record is nothing to scoff at.
He was brilliant for the Red Sox during their playoff run in 2021 that saw him come out of the bullpen in the American League Division Series against the Rays before he twirled five innings of one-run ball against the eventual World Series champion Astros in Game 4 of the AL Championship Series. And, of course, he held the Cubs to just two runs over five innings and struck out nine in Game 1 of the Wild Card Series last year, capping off an excellent first season in San Diego.
That Chicago lineup will be a little different this time -- much stronger, for one. He’ll have to navigate a top of the order that includes the likely NL MVP in center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong and a surging Alex Bregman, who posted a 1.010 OPS in the second half.
“It's a whole lineup; they make good contact, they don't swing outside of the zone,” Pivetta said. “They have guys in there that jell really well together, led by Bregman. It's just trying to keep them off-balance, but always sticking to my strengths and doing what I do best and just see where that night goes.”
Pivetta is up for the challenge.
“I'm healthy, I'm feeling good and I'm excited for the next step,” he said.

item.description: It’s do or die for the Phillies on Wednesday. item.content:encoded:
It’s do or die for the Phillies on Wednesday.
The Braves pushed them to the brink in Game 1 of the National League Wild Card with a 5-3 decision prompted by Austin Riley’s three-run shot in the eighth inning.
Another win in this series would mark first time the Braves prevailed over their NL East rivals in the postseason: the Phillies took the NLDS in both 2022 and 2023 and the 1993 NLCS over Atlanta.
This Phillies’ core has been chasing after a World Series throughout the decade, and another early exit will have its ramifications.
The onus to avoid that comes down to no one more than Bryce Harper, who struck out twice and went hitless Tuesday.
Phillies vs. Braves Game 2 prediction, best bet
Harper, who is a .269 postseason hitter in 58 games, narrowly missed a go-ahead two-run home run against Chris Sale in the sixth inning when the ball just sailed just right of the right-field pole.
He gets the lefty vs. righty matchup advantage against Atlanta’s Tyler Mahle, against whom he has posted a healthy .278/.350/.500 slash line.
Mahle leans on his four-seamer for nearly half of his pitches. He doesn’t throw it with extreme movement or overpowering velocity, averaging 92 mph, but he locates the strike zone with it well.
In the 14 four-seamers that Mahle served to Harper this season, Harper knocked two hits with a home run on eight swings, according to Statcast. Only two were whiffs.
In fact, Mahle wasn’t much of a swing-and-miss pitcher at all, ranking in only the 31 percentile.
That’s all while Harper remained an elite contact hitter, posting a .379 xwOBA, a Statcast metric that measures expected offensive production based on the exit velocity and launch angle of his contact rather than the results.
Harper has stated he loves playing at Truist Park, and his numbers say why.

- Learn all about How to Bet on Baseball
The two-time MVP hit .320 there in 27 plate appearances this season, which included a pair of home runs and five multi-base games out of six.
As the clubhouse leader, Harper was adamant about how the Phillies need to “finish the job” this postseason after having been here before.
He’ll have no choice but to deliver on that statement Wednesday.

item.title: [MLB.com] Riley flips Game 1 with 8th-inning blast on 99.9 mph pitch from Phillies' closer
item.dc:creator: Mark Bowman
item.description: ATLANTA -- Austin Riley supported Chris Sale’s strong start, halted the Phillies’ postseason dominance of Atlanta and put six months of frustration behind him with a swing that could make October worth savoring for both him and the Braves. Riley’s three-run homer off All-Star closer Jhoan Duran with two outs in the eighth inning gave the Braves a thrilling 5-3 win over the Phillies in Game 1 of the National League Wild Card Series on Tuesday afternoon at Truist Park. “I’m happy for Austin Riley,
item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA -- Austin Riley supported Chris Sale’s strong start, halted the Phillies’ postseason dominance of Atlanta and put six months of frustration behind him with a swing that could make October worth savoring for both him and the Braves.
Riley’s three-run homer off All-Star closer Jhoan Duran with two outs in the eighth inning gave the Braves a thrilling 5-3 win over the Phillies in Game 1 of the National League Wild Card Series on Tuesday afternoon at Truist Park.
“I’m happy for Austin Riley,” Braves manager Walt Weiss said. “It’s been a tough year for him. But this just goes to show you, when the playoffs start, everything starts at zero. Nothing that happened in the regular season really matters. It’s a clean slate. Austin Riley has been a great postseason player.”
Four of Riley’s six career postseason homers have been of the go-ahead variety and three of those have been hit in the eighth inning or later. That eighth inning or later total matches Troy Glaus, Bernie Williams, Jose Altuve and Freddie Freeman for the most in MLB history.
The slugging third baseman previously hit a go-ahead shot in the ninth inning of Game 1 of the NLCS on Oct. 12, 2020, and he hit a go-ahead two-run home run with two outs in the bottom of the eighth in Game 2 of the 2023 NLDS, also against the Phillies. Chipper Jones is the only other Braves player with multiple go-ahead homers in the eighth inning or later of a postseason game.
“I know how my season went,” Riley said. “It’s not the way I wanted it to. But that's the beauty of the postseason. You get a clean slate and go out there and try to do something for the boys and for this city.”
Instead of talking about being on the brink of elimination, the Braves joyfully discussed how everything changed when Riley sent Duran’s 99.9 mph fastball over the right-center-field fence for a go-ahead home run.
Riley doesn’t remember what any of his teammates said after he returned to a jubilant dugout after his home run. Was he also in a haze as he rounded the bases?
“I remember my gum falling out of my mouth,” Riley said.
It was a jaw-dropping moment that put the Braves in an encouraging position.
In the history of the best-of-three Wild Card Series, teams taking a 1-0 lead have gone on to win the series 21 of 24 times (88%), including 17 two-game sweeps. Home teams have won all nine series in which they have gone ahead 1-0, including eight sweeps.
The Phillies had won six of the previous eight postseason games played against the Braves this decade. Philadelphia beat Atlanta in the 2022 and ‘23 NL Division Series.
“It doesn't get more fun than this, playing this game in the postseason,” Weiss said. “You can imagine going from losing the lead to something like that. The swinging emotions are enormous. What a big home run.”
Sale played a significant role in this crucial Game 1 victory. The Braves ace registered nine strikeouts over 6 1/3 innings. Two of the three runs he surrendered came via a J.T. Realmuto triple that Didier Fuentes surrendered with two outs in the seventh.
So where was Sale when the value of his strong effort was preserved by Riley’s home run?
“I was getting some arm care in, and unfortunately the [clubhouse] TV I was watching was on the delay [feed],” he said. “I just heard craziness coming from the entire clubhouse. Everyone's losing their mind, and I'm just sitting there like, ‘Oh, what's going on?’ About four seconds later, you see what happened. I just couldn't be happier for him.”
Coming off two injury-shortened seasons, Riley hit .219 with 19 homers and a .654 OPS during the regular season. Safe to say this was the most frustrating season of the two-time All-Star’s career. This past weekend in Miami, he talked about how relaxing his right shoulder might have helped him hit two homers in last week’s Reds series.
The triple came against a 98.2 mph splitter that was in the middle of the zone. The ball had 109 mph exit velocity and it traveled a Statcast-projected 394 feet.
This home run came against a 99.9 mph four-seamer that was middle in. This is the hardest-thrown pitch Riley has homered against in his career, besting a homer he hit against Jacob deGrom’s 99.7 mph heater on July 1, 2021.
This latest home run had a 104.6 mph exit velocity and it traveled a projected 385 feet.
It would have been a home run in 27 of 30 MLB ballparks. Did Riley know it was gone?
“No, I did not,” he said. “I was just praying as I was running to first.”

item.content:encoded:
Welcome to the 2026 MLB playoffs, baseball fans. The postseason got started Tuesday with a quartet of Game 1s in the best-of-three Wild Card Series. The Braves came back against the Phillies in the early start, while the White Sox cruised to an easy win against the Astros and . In the late slate, Michael King took a no-hitter into the seventh inning en route to a blowout Padres win over the Cubs.
In these short series, the Game 1 winners are one victory away from the LDS round, and the Game 1 losers are one loss away from their season being over.
The Rays, Guardians, Brewers and Dodgers all secured byes and await the winners in the next round. The Rays are the American League's top seed and will face a division rival in the ALDS, whether it's the Yankees or the Red Sox. The Guardians, despite an 85-77 record that ranks 10th out of the 12 playoff teams, earned the No. 2 seed in the AL and will face either the 84-win White Sox or 81-win Astros in the next round.
The Brewers (103 wins) and Dodgers (100 wins) both hit triple digits in the win column in the regular season, and they will host NLDS Game 1s on Saturday. The Brewers get the Padres-Cubs winner, while the two-time reigning champion Dodgers get either the Braves or the Phillies.

item.content:encoded:
JustPredictions
Justice editors predict the upcoming year of sports.
Ben Khayat ’28: Only one Big Ten team will make the College Football Playoffs. The sample size is small, but the Big Ten has been downright shameful to start the 2026 season. The obvious examples are the Michigan Wolverines coming back from the dead to prevent a home loss to the Western Michigan Broncos, and the Rutgers Scarlet Knights succumbing to the UMass Minutemen, a team that didn’t win a single game last season. The rest of the conference hasn’t been much better. The Oregon Ducks came into the season ranked #2 in the country, but came up limping in their one-score win over the Boise State Broncos before getting dispatched by Oklahoma State on Saturday. The Ohio State Buckeyes led 23-3 against the Texas Longhorns, only to allow 21 unanswered points and choke what would have been the first statement win the conference has had this season. Come January, I can’t imagine many of these “top” teams will have impressed anybody enough to get an at-large bid over some other power conference opponents.
Luca D. Jordan ’28: The Chicago Bears will make the Superbowl this season. After having an amazing breakout season under head coach Ben Johnson and making their first playoff appearance since 2020, the Chicago Bears have shown explosive growth with a new offensive direction. Defined by their comeback wins, the Bears almost clinched the semi-finals last season, but quarterback Caleb Williams threw a bad pass that led to an interception against the Los Angeles Rams. Despite an unfortunate play that ended his season early, Williams has shown flashes of an all time great quarterback. When it comes down to the last few seconds, Williams is known to perform herculean throws to save the game. Although their offseason wasn’t particularly exciting, expect a surprising surge in performance across the board from the entire roster. Previous champs Seattle Seahawks are dead in the water without Sam Darnold and the Rams have added some big names to their roster, but it’s just stars over substance. The Bears have a few decades of an underdog legacy behind them, and that’s too much destiny to ignore.
Bryan Wolfe ’27: The New York Knicks are running it back! I have faith. Even though the Philadelphia 76ers have the starting five of doom and despair, I believe in the king of New York Jalen Brunson to lead us back to the promised land.
Chava Thiell ’29: Alexander Zverev will finish the 2026 ATP season with an ATP finals win and the World #1 ranking. As unfortunate as it may be for diehard Sincaraz fans, Jannik Sinner isn’t healthy and Carlos Alcaraz is still adjusting to his return to tennis after a four-month hiatus. After Zverev clinched two Slams this year, his momentum cannot seem to be stopped. Conversely, I think Aryba Sabalenka will walk away with the WTA Finals trophy, inspired by a heartbreaking US Open final loss to rival Elena Rybakina and a mission to come away from the season with a big tournament win.
Eli Sandalow ’28: The New England Patriots will go 4-13. Drake Maye looks like he regressed, AJ Brown is prone to long-term injuries and Rhamondre Stevenson is one of the most overrated running backs in the NFL right now.
Alyssa Wu ‘29: The Dodgers won’t three-peat this year.The Dodgers have a stacked lineup, with Shohei Ohtani, Freddie Freeman and Mookie Betts, plus a star-studded starting rotation of Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow. Along with their veterans, new acquisitions this year include stars like Tarik Skubal, a two-time American League Cy Young winner. Despite this, the Dodgers have not dominated through the season as many expected. They went 13-14 in August, though they have found their footing again in September. Injuries raise more concerns; Ohtani only returned to the lineup on September 23 after a stint on the injured list and is not expected to pitch for the remainder of the season. Reliever Blake Treinen, who has helped bring three championships to the Dodgers in his six seasons, suffered a season-ending injury on September 26. With Kyle Tucker and Andy Pages being the only starting position players under the age of 30, the question is whether these Dodger veterans will be healthy and as productive as they used to be during the postseason. The MLB Playoff bracket itself does not always reward the ‘best’ team. The Dodgers in 2022 are one of the clearest examples of this. In 2022, they went 111-51 and won 14 of 19 regular-season games against the Padres. However, after winning Game 1 of the NLDS, they lost three straight to the San Diego Padres, ending their season. The postseason can bring plenty of surprises, and a team’s regular season does not always predict its success in the playoffs. The Dodgers had to come back from a 3-2 deficit to win last year’s World Series, and this year’s team seems to be much more vulnerable. The Dodgers are sure to make it far in the playoffs, but another championship is far from guaranteed.

item.title: [sfexaminer.com] No matter who wins, MLB will push salary cap
item.dc:creator: Ken Rosenthal; The Athletic
item.description: (Commentary) Here's the thing about all the agita related to the Los Angeles Dodgers, MLB's competitive balance and the 2026 postseason: No outcome this October will change the calculus for the team owners. Even if the small-market Milwaukee Brewers, Tampa Bay Rays or Cleveland Guardians win the World Series, the league will continue its push for a salary cap, contending the sport lacks sufficient parity and is effectively broken. Not that long ago, the league was making precisely the opposite a
item.content:encoded:
(Commentary)
Here's the thing about all the agita related to the Los Angeles Dodgers, MLB's competitive balance and the 2026 postseason: No outcome this October will change the calculus for the team owners.
Even if the small-market Milwaukee Brewers, Tampa Bay Rays or Cleveland Guardians win the World Series, the league will continue its push for a salary cap, contending the sport lacks sufficient parity and is effectively broken.
Not that long ago, the league was making precisely the opposite argument. Its public-relations department, in news releases before the 2021 and 2022 seasons, described competitive balance as a hallmark of MLB.
Let's be clear: Revenue disparity between large- and small-market clubs is a legitimate concern. The league and players union need to adopt significant measures to make the playing field more level. But the league's argument for greater competitive balance, if not a red herring, is at least an argument of convenience. And not a particularly strong one, if you watched the regular season.
The Brewers finished with the best record in the National League. The Rays produced the best record in the American League. And the Guardians became the third small-market team to earn one of four first-round byes. Perhaps the Guardians were undeserving, considering their record was only the 11th best in the majors. But by finishing with the second-best mark among AL division winners, they clinched the bye under the postseason format the league and union created.
So is the sport really that far gone?
The league's own news release in 2022 noted that MLB produced 15 different World Series champions in the prior 21 seasons. The Texas Rangers in 2023 made it 16. And before the 2024 World Series, MLB Commissioner Rob Manfred told The Athletic, "Our record on competitive balance is darn good."
Just two years later, to hear Manfred & Co. tell it, the sport is having an existential crisis. All because the league's highest-revenue team, the Dodgers, won back-to-back World Series. All because the team owners want to build their case for a cap.
The league cites a need for greater competitive balance as justification to drastically overhaul the game's economic system. And it is trumpeting a new set of facts -- specifically, the absence of a small-market champion since the 2015 Kansas City Royals -- to make its case.
There is no denying that in that time, large-market teams have accounted for 90% of World Series winners, 85% of World Series participants and 77.5% of league championship series participants. And sure, the same pattern might continue this year.
Never mind that the Dodgers performed below expectations in the regular season for the second consecutive year. According to FanGraphs, they still stand the best chance of winning the World Series -- 36.7%, with the Brewers next at 11.6%. As if on cue, and in some cases by design, the Dodgers' best players are getting healthy and rounding into form.
If Los Angeles becomes the first team since the 1998 to 2000 New York Yankees to win three consecutive World Series titles, the league will surely use that data point in its pitch that only a salary cap can save the sport.
And if the Brewers or Rays win their first Series, or if the Guardians win their first since 1948? The league will consider it an aberration, a single-season outcome that means little when compared with the larger sample size of the previous 10 seasons. An exception that proves the rule.
But let's broaden the discussion.
By emphasizing postseason results, the league is devaluing the most accurate measure of a club, the six-month grind of the regular season. Not to mention devaluing the 162 games of inventory all 30 clubs must sell.
Since 2015 -- the line of demarcation the league has set with the Royals' World Series triumph -- the Guardians rank fourth in regular-season wins, the Brewers fifth and the Rays seventh. They are models for other small-market teams, proof that those clubs do not have to operate without hope.
It's true none of those teams won a World Series in the past 10 years. But the Rays got there in the shortened 2020 season. The Guardians reached the American League Championship Series in 2024, the Brewers in 2025. Inferior depth, resulting in part from lower payrolls, might be part of the reason none went further. Adjustments to the collective bargaining agreement could help address that.
No reasonable person would start a league from scratch and adopt baseball's current economic system, in which the league says that the top four spenders -- the Dodgers, New York Mets, Yankees and Philadelphia Phillies -- outspent the bottom 22 in free agency over the course of the current labor agreement.
Reasonable people can disagree, however, whether a cap is the only possible solution when the players' historic opposition to the concept might lead to the cancellation of part or all of the 2027 season.
The league keeps referencing polls saying fans want a cap. Fans, though, evidently are not too upset with the current state of affairs: The league's attendance increased again this year, reaching its highest level since 2016.
Even in cap sports, not every team begins every season with the expectation of competing for a title. The most successful franchises are the shrewdest. Part of baseball's problem is that innovative small-market clubs no longer hold the competitive advantage they once did over less forward-thinking opponents.
Ex // Top Stories
Some of the large-market teams plucked top small-market executives. Very few clubs, if any, continue to lag behind in the intellectual arms race. Even the Colorado Rockies and Washington Nationals, two of the slowest clubs to adapt to baseball's information age, have gotten smarter.
If everyone is essentially working off the same data, payrolls become more of a separator. But even then, the edge money provides is not an absolute guarantee of success in October.
Before winning in the shortened 2020 season, the Dodgers had not won a World Series since 1988. The Mets have not won since 1986. The Phillies and Yankees are experiencing championship droughts that began in 2008 and 2009.
Many baseball executives consider the postseason a crapshoot, fearing the random outcomes that occur in small samples.
The Dodgers, without question, have inordinate financial advantages, including the right to withhold a healthy portion of their massive local TV deal from revenue sharing, a benefit that arose from a settlement the league reached in bankruptcy court with the team's former owner Frank McCourt.
Still, the Dodgers in 2022 and 2023 were eliminated in the division series by rivals from smaller markets, the San Diego Padres and Arizona Diamondbacks. In 2024, the Dodgers' first year with Shohei Ohtani, they nearly lost to the Padres again in division series play. And if not for a series of fortuitous events, they would have lost the 2025 World Series to the Toronto Blue Jays.
Another thing lost in the discussion about the Dodgers' dominance is that villains are good for business. This is the third consecutive season the Dodgers led the majors in road attendance. Their spending forces other NL clubs to try to keep pace. The small-market Padres, in particular, are better for it.
Yet the ability to spend is sometimes a double-edged sword. Long-term contracts sometimes backfire. Seemingly capable of papering over any mistake by simply printing more money, the Dodgers roll merrily along even when free-agent additions such as Kyle Tucker, Edwin Díaz and Tanner Scott slump. But several of the Dodgers' biggest and most expensive stars are facing age-related decline. A number of other top-10 payroll clubs, including the Padres, are locked into the same kinds of players.
None of that means that the league and union should proceed as if all is well, assuming the game's cyclical nature will balance things out. The concerns of the small-market clubs must be addressed, and the union acknowledged as much in May with its initial proposals, some of which addressed revenue disparity.
The union proposed enhanced revenue sharing that included protections "to ensure clubs prioritize winning over profiteering"; financial rewards for successful revenue-sharing recipients and draft-pick incentives for them to sign free agents and retain their own players on the verge of hitting the open market.
The league scoffed at the union proposals, as one might expect with the collective bargaining agreement months away from expiration and the parties holding completely different worldviews. Finding a middle ground will be tricky. At least to this point, large-market clubs are willing to share more revenue -- and yield their inherent financial advantages -- but only under a cap system that fixes their costs.
Teams like the Brewers, Rays and Guardians clearly do not require more money to win regular-season games. But the way they operate, frequently trading stars as they get closer to free agency, is far from fan-friendly. Brewers fans buying a Jacob Misiorowski jersey and Rays fans buying a Junior Caminero jersey know not to get too attached to those players. As one small-market executive says: "Championships are won with talent, continuity and experience. We can get talent. The other two are tough to come by."
Tough, but not impossible. Countless examples exist of revenue-sharing recipients signing homegrown players for the long term. The Brewers did it with Jackson Chourio, Cooper Pratt and Luis Lara, the Guardians with José Ramírez and Tanner Bibee. The Pittsburgh Pirates might not keep Paul Skenes, but they locked up Konnor Griffin. The Royals secured extensions with Bobby Witt Jr. and Maikel Garcia, the Seattle Mariners with Cal Raleigh and Julio Rodríguez, the Arizona Diamondbacks with Corbin Carroll and Geraldo Perdomo.
Based on its proposals, the union thinks giving small-market teams an even better opportunity to retain players would benefit the sport. A salary cap is not necessary to make those adjustments and others to the collective bargaining agreement. Much as the league would like fans to believe otherwise, this is not an all-or-nothing situation.
In June, a reporter asked Manfred why he portrays a league he described in 2024 as having a "darn good" record on competitive balance to be out of whack just two years later.
"In the context, particularly of the postseason, where you're trying to generate interest and maximize viewership, I think it's important to emphasize competitiveness," Manfred said. "And there are aspects of competitiveness."
He added: "When we think about it from a labor perspective, we're focused on an entirely different part of the calendar. And that's the offseason, when you're trying to sell season tickets, and the perception among our fans that's really strong that we have a lack of competitiveness."
Maximizing viewership in the postseason? Viewership in the United States last year was the sport's highest since 2017. Selling season tickets? Sure, it's a problem in markets where team owners do not adequately invest in their franchises. It should be less of a problem in places like Milwaukee, Tampa Bay and Cleveland, if we're just talking about the product.
Make the current system fairer, and those clubs will stand even better chances of reaching a postseason that the league expanded to 12 teams from 10 in 2022. Give those clubs enough cracks at the postseason, and eventually one or more will break through.
It could happen this year, if the Brewers, Rays or Guardians win the World Series. The system needs improvement, no doubt. But if competitive balance is the object, it's a lot closer than it appears.

item.title: [NBC Sports Philadelphia] What's different about these Phillies? Bryce Harper, Trea Turner weigh in
item.dc:creator: Cole Weintraub
item.description: ATLANTA — Yes, these Phillies. The same core that has reached the postseason five consecutive years, yet hasn't won a playoff series since 2023, has another opportunity to finish what it started. But Bryce Harper sees some differences in this version of the Phillies, even if many of the names are familiar. item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA — Yes, these Phillies.
The same core that has reached the postseason five consecutive years, yet hasn't won a playoff series since 2023, has another opportunity to finish what it started.
But Bryce Harper sees some differences in this version of the Phillies, even if many of the names are familiar.
"I think they're different, but they have a little bit of the same DNA," Harper said Monday at Truist Park. "We have a lot of the same and similar DNA that we've had the last couple years, with a sprinkle of a couple other guys."
Those additions, along with the growth of several returning players, could help determine whether Philadelphia's latest postseason appearance ends differently from its previous two.
The most obvious change is in the bullpen.
Over the last two postseasons, Phillies relievers have combined for a 6.82 ERA, a 1.65 WHIP and six home runs allowed in 30 1/3 innings. Their ERA jumps to 11.42 when pitching with a lead.
News
Those numbers help explain why Philadelphia hasn't advanced beyond the NLDS in either of its last two appearances.
This year's relief group looks considerably different. José Alvarado is the only remaining member of the Phillies' 2023 bullpen, and after posting a 5.86 ERA this season, he isn't expected to handle the most important late-inning assignments.
Instead, Philadelphia has Jhoan Duran at the back end, with Jonathan Bowlan, Alex McFarlane and Chase Shugart among the newer faces who could be asked to get the ball to their closer.
The Phillies haven't seen how this group will respond together in October. That uncertainty leaves them with questions, but at least they'll be trying to solve a familiar problem with a different group of pitchers.
The offense, meanwhile, has undergone fewer changes. Philadelphia still relies heavily on Harper, Kyle Schwarber and Trea Turner, with Alec Bohm and Bryson Stott providing much of the production behind them.
And that group has something to prove.
Of the 12 teams that played multiple postseason series across 2024 and 2025, the Phillies had the lowest batting average, the lowest average with runners in scoring position and the highest chase rate.
Too often, Philadelphia has struggled to put the ball in play when it has an opportunity to score. It was one of the reasons the club acquired Luis Arraez in August, but a left ankle sprain suffered during the final week of the regular season will keep him off the Wild Card roster.
That puts more responsibility on the returning hitters to sustain rallies against an Atlanta pitching staff that begins the series with Chris Sale and Tyler Mahle.
Bohm and Stott enter the postseason swinging the bat well, something Turner believes reflects the growth he's witnessed within the clubhouse this year.
"I think it was just kind of cool to see guys struggle at times and then pull themselves out of it at times," Turner said. "It didn't go as well as it could have gone for a lot of us."
He pointed specifically to Bohm, whose difficult start gave way to a productive final several months.
"He's been such a good player for a long time, and then this second half or the last two-thirds of the season, he's been really, really good for us," Turner said.
But the Phillies have also introduced a different kind of hitter into the lower part of their lineup.
Justin Crawford, who made his major league debut earlier this season, has given Philadelphia another player capable of reaching base, putting pressure on the defense and delivering in important situations.
From June 14 through the end of the regular season, Crawford hit .294, the 15th-highest average in baseball among players who appeared in at least 80 games during that span. He ranked third among rookies who met that qualification.
His production with runners in scoring position was even more striking.
Crawford hit .491 in those situations over that stretch, the highest average among 109 players who met the same games-played requirement. His 1.131 OPS with runners in scoring position ranked fifth.
He won't necessarily start every postseason game. Crawford shares center-field duties with Derek Hill, whose speed, defense and production against left-handed pitching give interim manager Don Mattingly another way to construct his lineup.
Hill has made quite an impression on Harper.
"He's just a professional, I would say. He's got a professional mindset," Harper said. "Obviously having his pops, coming from a big-league family, I think that helps a lot."
Harper went a step further when discussing Hill's arrival, which came in a June trade with the Chicago White Sox.
"I think it's one of the better moves Dave has made for our organization bringing him in," Harper said, referring to president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski.
His praise extended well beyond Hill's production. Harper singled out the way the outfielder prepares, backs up bases, looks for opportunities to advance and helps Philadelphia's younger players.
"He's a gamer. He plays the game the right way, and you need guys like that on your team," Harper said.
Hill is also part of a trio that has developed a close bond away from the field.
Along with Bryan De La Cruz and Edmundo Sosa, he belongs to "Team Blessed," a group built around their shared faith and a competitive batting-cage routine during games. All three have contributed in important moments throughout the season, frequently coming off the bench without the benefit of regular at-bats.
Harper mentioned Hill and De La Cruz specifically when asked what makes this club different from previous Phillies postseason teams. Both have given Philadelphia additional options against left-handed pitching, something it lacked earlier in the year.
And Harper believes players in those supporting roles can end up being the ones everyone remembers.
"It's funny to look back on a lot of postseasons in baseball history," Harper said. "Not many of the superstar players play to their ability."
Harper himself is a notable exception.
Among the 109 hitters in postseason history with at least 200 plate appearances, his .986 OPS ranks third, trailing only Carlos Beltrán and Albert Pujols. His .596 slugging percentage is fourth.
But his point wasn't about the stars who have delivered in October. It was about the players whose contributions nobody saw coming.
Consider Travis Ishikawa, a part-time first baseman who found himself playing left field for the 2014 San Francisco Giants. In Game 5 of the NLCS, Ishikawa hit a three-run, walk-off homer against the Cardinals to send San Francisco to the World Series.
That's the type of player Harper had in mind when discussing Philadelphia's reserves.
"You never know who the October hero is going to be," Harper said. "Then you get to the end and you're like, man, that guy had a great postseason and you might never hear from him again."
Hill, De La Cruz, Sosa and Crawford will have opportunities to write their own postseason stories. For some, it will be their first chance to experience an October environment that Harper knows well.
His advice is to avoid treating it as a different game.
"All the work that you put in during the season and all the work that you put in to get you to this point, all that doesn't matter," Harper said. "It's the same game that we've been playing. It just might get a little bit quicker or might speed up on you a little bit if you let it."
That doesn't mean the veteran slugger wants his younger teammates to ignore the occasion.
"If you can really try to just enjoy the moment, I don't know, you could go 0-for-4 tomorrow or you could go 0-for-5 tomorrow or you can go 3-for-4 with two homers and win a game," Harper said. "If you just really take in the moment, take in the opportunity, there's no greater feeling."
The Phillies have considerable postseason experience, but this season has tested them in ways their more recent teams haven't necessarily encountered.
They began 9-19, underwent a managerial change and spent much of the year rearranging their pitching staff because of injuries and inconsistent performances.
There are similarities to 2022, when Philadelphia also changed managers after a difficult start before making an improbable run to the World Series. That team didn't secure its postseason berth until Oct. 3 and entered the playoffs having gone 11-14 in September.
Turner wasn't part of that club. He joined the Phillies the following offseason, and much of what stood out to him about this year's team had less to do with the final results than the way his teammates responded to their own struggles.
He recalled a recent conversation about Schwarber, who was still working through issues with his swing during the final days of the regular season.
"He's hit 380 homers in his career, and one of the best hitters in the game, and he's just not satisfied," Turner said.
For Turner, that restlessness says something about the veteran players who have been together through several disappointing postseason exits.
"Just seeing guys kind of manage their situations and want to compete and want to get back out there and just loving the game, I think that was pretty cool from a team standpoint," he said.
It's a perspective that comes from watching the same players through different stages of their careers. As Harper acknowledged, they're getting older. Stott has grown into a more established hitter, Bohm's future in Philadelphia is uncertain, and the club has brought in new players to complement a core that has been trying to win a championship for years.
The Phillies have invested heavily in their starting rotation, traded for a closer last year they believe can handle the biggest innings and introduced players who could give their offense a different look. But much of their postseason success will still depend on familiar names producing in situations where they've struggled before.
Harper, now preparing for his ninth postseason in 15 major league seasons, understands how rare those opportunities can become.
He brought up Hall-of-Fame quarterback Dan Marino, who reached the Super Bowl early in his career but never returned, as an example of how little a player's previous success guarantees about what comes next.
The Phillies have reached October five straight years. That doesn't mean they'll keep getting chances.
"I'm very lucky," Harper said. "Obviously I haven't got to the point where I want to be or our team hasn't either, but just to be in these moments, just to be given the opportunity to be here, I'm so grateful for that. It motivates me to get to these points."
Philadelphia arrives in Atlanta with many of the same stars, some new faces and the experience of a regular season that nearly slipped away from it.
Harper knows what he wants this group to accomplish. But after all the postseason games he's played, he's learned there's no telling which teammate might deliver the moment that gets them there.
"It's a cool opportunity for a lot of guys that have never played here," he said. "You could end up being a hero after having just an absolute terrible year."
Push for the playoffs coverage on NBC Sports Philadelphia is presented by Toyota, proud partner of the Philadelphia Phillies.
